Its primary function is to determine the time of day by observing a shadow's length and orientation, which shifts consistently with the passage of time. For centuries, scholars and astronomers have leveraged these shadows to study celestial bodies and planetary movements. The advent of modern technology has streamlined traditional sundial mechanisms, making them highly popular among researchers and students in the field of electronics. The objective of this modern sundial project is to design a low-cost, efficient device that automatically calculates and displays the time. This innovative tool holds significant potential for educational institutions, including high schools and universities. The core of the proposed solution relies on detecting the shadow cast by an obstacle in front of the sundial; the shadow's duration and orientation consistently correspond to the time. Technically, the project will be built around a sensor array designed to detect an object's shadow (referred to as a "light obstacle") across various lighting conditions. This sensor will focus on a specific area of a defined surface to measure the light intensity and direction of the incoming "light obstacle." Consequently, the project will generate data regarding the sun's position in the sky, including the movement and position of shadow obstacles relative to the sundial. This information will be stored in memory to compute and display the time. The proposed solution will be implemented using microcontrollers (such as an Arduino), computer vision algorithms, and a liquid crystal display (LCD). Ultimately, the core of this innovation is a sensor that functions like the retina of an electronic eye, enabling the identification of an obstacle's light orientation and the consistent tracking of its shadow's movement.

which integrates digital entertainment and education with second-order differential equations. In this framework, players assume the roles of vectors within a vector field. The objective is to reach a target point $P$ originating from a starting point $S$. This goal is achieved by manipulating a parameter that influences the orbit's curvature; specifically, lower parameter values result in more circular paths, while higher values produce routes with greater number of oscillations.

Mathematically, the trajectory of a player is described by a second-order differential equation. When the vector field is conservative and derived from a potential energy function that follows an inverse-square law—similar to the force exerted by a point mass—the system exhibits an energy integral, serving as a first integral of the equation.

We demonstrate that if the vector field's intensity is constant or increasing with distance from the origin, a player beginning from rest at any point $S$ can reach the target point $P$ through an appropriate vector choice. However, if the intensity increases initially and then decreases, reaching the target is impossible under rest conditions.

Additionally, we examine the case where players start with non-zero velocity vectors. Under this scenario, and provided the vector intensity at the target point is zero, it is possible to connect the target point with the starting point even when the energy constant is positive, a situation that differs significantly from the case where starting velocity is zero. Finally, drawing inspiration from the Kepler problem, we analyze the evolution of the vector parameter over time. Our findings indicate that a player can gradually increase the parameter to reduce oscillations in their orbit.

Throughout this study, we emphasize the vector choice problem from an applied mathematics perspective. Furthermore, illustrating the development of the vector parameter, we examine the connection between a vector intensity function and the existence of first integrals for second-order differential equations. Lastly, comparative tables are presented to highlight the uniqueness of players in this DED2D context.

We demonstrate that for any such sentence $\Phi$, there exists a corresponding sentence $\Phi'$ utilizing the same variable count but relying solely on one symmetric binary relation, such that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is linearly proportional to that of $\Phi$. Furthermore, all models of $\Phi'$ are bipartite graphs. As a consequence, we establish that the distinction between linear and non-linear spectra remains meaningful even when restricted to sentences with three variables. Finally, we apply this approach to re-demonstrate that every context-free language is isomorphic to a first-order language's spectrum, while also providing a novel method to derive a lower bound of $\log |\QQ|$, where $\QQ$ represents the set of $\Phi$'s queries (cardinalities). To our knowledge, this remains the sole existing technique capable of generating lower bounds of this nature. Additionally, we analyze several open questions concerning the limitations of this method. Specifically, we demonstrate that it can be leveraged to construct a first-order language with three variables whose spectrum includes all context-free languages, alongside a sufficiently large set of prime numbers, and whose model sizes remain proportional to the length of the underlying context-free grammar. We further confirm that the three-variable constraint is essential for this result and explore extensions to higher variable counts. Moreover, we illustrate that this framework recovers Knuth's classical result regarding the linearity of spectra: namely, that every context-free language that is not also a regular language contains an infinite set of cardinalities comprising at least one representative from each equivalence class defined by division. We also note that our technique remains applicable to the study of hypergraphs. In this context, we show that the linear vs. nonlinear distinction remains significant even when limiting the number of hypergraph edges per model to three. This follows because every structure with three colored edges can be represented as a bipartite hypergraph employing only three vectors of size two. Like the binary relation case, sufficiently large models are required; specifically, exponential size relative to the sentence length. This is necessary because the number of possible bipartite hypergraphs with three edges can far exceed that of bipartite graphs when edges are permitted to be empty. We conclude by presenting multiple insights into the methodology of Blass and Lubarsky, who were the first to prove that all context-free languages can be realized as spectra of structures with a constant number of binary relations and linear-sized models

This study derives a semi-analytical formula for the dynamical density-density linear-response function (the "Lindhard" function) of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions at finite temperatures. This result is essential for characterizing the finite-temperature screening of interacting massless Dirac fermions within the Random Phase Approximation. Specifically, we utilize this formula to generate quantitative predictions for the specific heat and compressibility of doped graphene sheets. Our findings indicate that at low temperatures, the specific heat exhibits the standard linear-in-temperature behavior typical of a normal Fermi liquid, with the slope determined exclusively by the renormalized quasiparticle velocity. In contrast, at higher temperatures, the slope becomes nonlinear, a direct consequence of the doping-independent, semicircular density-of-states component inherent in Dirac fermion systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the relative importance of semicircular vs. quadratic low-energy quasiparticles, regarding specific heat and compressibility, is controlled by the ratio of the chemical potential to the Fermi temperature. Finally, we show that these theoretical predictions align well with existing semi-analytical and numerical results for the density-density response function of interacting massless Dirac fermions at zero temperature. These insights are expected to be valuable in analyzing the thermodynamic properties of doped graphene. Relatedly, our derived Lindhard formula for massless Dirac fermions at finite temperatures may prove useful in other contexts involving response theory for Dirac fermions. This work is part of a related study [arXiv:1305.4081] concerning the temperature dependence of the interaction strength in graphene. This limitation arises because such systems fail to capture speech at a continuous temporal fine-grained level. Consequently, this paper introduces WaveNet-TSS, a novel end-to-end neural speech synthesis architecture that achieves continuous prosodic features throughout the generated speech. We extend this methodology to allow the pooled posterior to serve as the reference, enabling the comparison of any two submodels. This approach is fundamentally guaranteed to prevent projection predictive inference from yielding comparisons that contradict the full model's posterior. By utilizing the decomposability property of its expected loss function, we develop a computationally viable algorithm for comparing submodels. This algorithm operates by solving a system of linear equations, making it highly efficient for scenarios involving large variable sets. Unlike selection-based methods, our approach is guaranteed to produce no contradictions and is well-defined even when submodels cannot be separated into disjoint sets. Furthermore, the method remains robust in the presence of non-exchangeable data, a capability for which there is currently no equivalent alternative. A key advantage is that the procedure requires no arbitrary choices regarding subsets; users simply input two submodels of interest to receive the desired comparison. Our existing R package already supports this functionality. We validate the method's effectiveness through simulations and apply it to a single-cell RNA-sequencing gene network inference study. This analysis demonstrates the procedure's ability to identify substantial disagreements between submodels, revealing previously unrecognized substantial discrepancies between groups of genes with similar expression levels. By examining which variables drive the largest disagreements, we uncover which sets of variables are most conflicting. Furthermore, we show how to integrate existing pathway information to efficiently compare non-nested models, even when they are nested within larger models. This allows for the detection of pathway-level disagreements, which is critical for evaluating the compatibility of pathways. We illustrate this with experiments comparing groups of genes belonging to the same or different non-redundant pathways. Our results indicate that genes within a pathway are the most likely to disagree, with non-pathological pathways exhibiting the least disagreement. Finally, we investigate the single-cell gene network's complexity and the variation in disagreement levels across different gene types.

Unlike prior investigations focused solely on neutral scalar or pseudoscalar mediators coupling to top quarks, this work extends the scope to include vector mediators. Neutral current vector mediators are evaluated through the top quark + missing transverse momentum channel, while both neutral and charged vector mediators are examined using the top quark + missing $p_T$ algorithm. These findings also enable the exclusion of certain dark photon models constrained by little big bang nucleosynthesis and cosmic microwave background data. Although the probing limits of these methods can be theoretically lifted by measuring signals from scattered photons or electrons, the corresponding data analysis remains laborious and lacks both theoretical and practical foundations. This work demonstrates that the quantum speed limit of scattering processes directly lower-bounds the resolution attainable by any microscope, regardless of the detector used. We derive all necessary formulas to translate the fluctuations recorded by a specific detector into the achieved resolution and discuss multiple detector configurations to illustrate how to push the boundaries of what is possible. We apply these principles to determine the resolution limits of X-ray and electron microscopes operating across various energy regimes, including nonlinear multiphoton electron microscopy of nanoscale objects illuminated by ultra-intense X-rays, where the attained resolution significantly surpasses conventional electron microscopy. Furthermore, these principles offer a framework to explore new methods for enhancing the resolution of existing microscopy technologies and to establish the fundamental limits of emerging quantum sensing approaches to structure. Finally, we address the theoretical notion of infinite-resolution imaging and its implications for the nature of matter at arbitrarily small length scales. These principles can be extended to any quantum system capable of scattering probes, making them applicable to studying the structure and interactions of matter at resolutions limited only by the uncertainty principle.

The velocity structure of the accretion flow plays a critical role in determining how mass transfers between stars. This study examines velocity structures in binary systems at 1 year and 10 years old using high-time-resolution hydrodynamic simulations that incorporate radiative radiation hydrodynamics. Results indicate that radiative effects are essential: accounting for radiation pressure significantly enhances accretion rates and instabilities compared to models ignoring these effects. Furthermore, when radiative radiation hydrodynamics is included, the mean velocity structure aligns more closely with high-resolution interferometric observations of young stellar clusters and multiple systems. At early ages, the dominant flow structure is a circumnuclear disk linking the binaries to the center of the collapsing cloud; this flow remains sub-Keplerian near the binaries and multiple ones. While this disk flow is nearly axisymmetric at radii originating from less than 1 au, it becomes increasingly turbulent and disordered at larger scales. Turbulence and angle-averaged velocity distributions at young ages are approximately half-Maxwellian, suggesting that velocity structures in young multiple systems are highly dependent on radiative radiation hydrodynamics. Considering both radiative transfer and turbulence, our findings indicate that velocity structures are more likely to channel angular momentum outward and internal to the binaries, thereby facilitating further accretion onto the young multiple systems. Finally, we demonstrate that velocity structures at ages of 1 year and 10 years can successfully explain recent Gaia kinematic data for young stars and multiple star systems within the Taurus-Auriga association. viable cosmological models. We demonstrate that they possess a natural geometric structure capable of describing inhomogeneous matter distributions arranged in a periodic pattern across space. We establish theorems regarding their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of Einstein's equations under these periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we identify a significant class of exact solutions that highlight the utility of such spacetimes in cosmology, exhibiting early-time behavior approaching homogeneity and isotropy, alongside late-time characteristics featuring peaks and voids in matter distribution. These solutions exhibit both light- and caustic-forming singularities, and the fluid dynamics are entirely consistent. Additionally, we find that similar periodic spacetimes can serve as effective dark energy models for our universe. In this context, the universe's expansion follows the observed pattern of initial deceleration followed by acceleration, with the energy density and pressure matching observational data. Finally, we examine the global properties of these spacetimes using the theory of globally hyperbolic manifolds. This framework enables the formulation and potential resolution of the initial value problem, alongside the potential to address final state questions. This represents the first application of these manifolds to general relativistic cosmology. Finally, we relate these spacetimes to other Einstein's equation solutions and discuss their potential astrophysical applications.

Keywords: Inhomogeneous cosmological models; Dark energy models; Global topology of spacetimes.

\endabstract \address \email \endaddress \section{Introduction} \subsection{Statement of the Problem} Our universe is spatially homogeneous, meaning all matter is distributed uniformly throughout space. However, this idealized assumption is an approximation that fails to account for the universe's well-documented small-scale inhomogeneities. These include stars, galaxies, clusters, and superclusters. To model this realistic matter distribution, our cosmological model must be inhomogeneous. This paper introduces spacetimes with effective inhomogeneous matter distributions that are, nevertheless, intrinsically flat, or at least very close to it. These spacetimes are not only physically plausible—because the flat spatial metric allows us to interpret gravitational effects as curvature in the time dimension, consistent with current understanding of spatial spatial curvature and dark energy—they also provide a fully non-linear resolution to the Einstein equations under these specific conditions. This marks a critical advancement over the development of inhomogeneous cosmological models, a topic we will elaborate on in the subsequent paragraphs.

Nuclei (AGNs) can be estimated via their fundamental frequency, which is linked to the quasi-polar modes of geodesic orbits with zero inclination ($i=0$) and zero radial action ($j_{\text{crit}}=0$). These modes govern low- inclination accretion streams and radiation from nearly axis-aligned spin-orbit interactions. Consequently, the relativistic pericenter precession rate for $i=0$ orbits near a black hole is determined by its parameters $\{M, a, i, e\}$. We demonstrate that the critical surface in parameter space, where the relativistic pericenter precession rate vanishes for $i=0$ geodesics, is defined by the condition $\{M, a\}$ satisfying $\sqrt{Q_0(x)}(1-4x)-2(2-5x)=0$, where $x=a/x$. This surface corresponds to the critical surface where the fundamental frequency becomes undefined for $i=0$ orbits. Furthermore, for $i=0$ geodesics, the fundamental frequency exhibits a pole (relativistic escape) at the location of this critical surface, with the Roberthsonian index approaching zero at the critical point and becoming negative elsewhere. Finally, we show that the Roberthsonian index can be expressed as a function of the fundamental frequency for $i=0$ geodesics. Although our analysis is restricted to $i=0$, the findings may extend to small non-zero inclinations. The Roberthsonian index offers an effective tool for characterizing the parameters of black holes that possess a fundamental frequency. This study examines how these agitated loops evolve over time using an ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation, focusing on magnetic field topology, wave activity, and particle acceleration. The simulation initializes with an ideal gas, radially symmetric, and field-free initial condition, incorporating both radial boundary driving and magnetic field boundary twisting. As these forces impart energy to the loops, they become magnetic free-energy rich and unstable to the (grad)-B instability, triggering magnetic reconnection and magnetic field generation. This initial field amplification drives an Alfvén wave cascade, which creates electron FDR heating and drives the magnetic field into the non-linear phase, thereby producing current-driven field particle heating. Ultimately, magnetic fields are generated around the loop legs, driving a second reconnection event at the loop bases and facilitating particle escape from the loop tops. These findings offer new insights into the magnetic field generation and the multi-specie non-thermal particle population observed during noise storms. Furthermore, the study provides a novel explanation for how topology and Agitated Loop Energy (ALE) give rise to noise storms without requiring pre-existing magnetic field topology. Finally, this work establishes a foundation for investigating the loop source of solar radio type III bursts.
Based on the magnetic field topology of narrow angle preflare loops, we simulate how the loop evolves over time, focusing on its Agitated Loop Energy (ALE) and the magnetic field topology around the loop base. Our results show that the Agitated Loop Energy initially concentrates near the loop top. Over time, this loop topology undergoes magnetic field reconnection, creating current-carrying loops. **I. INTRODUCTION** The magneto-optical trap (MOT) is a device that uses light and magnetic fields to capture and cool atoms to temperatures as low as a few micro-Kelvin (μK) [1]. As a fundamental component of many quantum technologies, the MOT is employed in quantum physics education, as well as in studies of quantum physics, engineering, and mathematics. Enhancing the performance, size, and cost-effectiveness of MOTs is therefore essential. The standard MOT utilizes six counter-propagating laser beams alongside a magnetic gradient produced by a cylindrical coil. Recent advances in planar optics have replaced the six beams with a single laser directed at a diffraction grating chip to create spatially modulated standing waves [4]. Similarly, flat coils have been developed to generate magnetic fields for various purposes [5]. In this work, we demonstrate a planar MOT by integrating these two grating-based coil designs. This novel trap combines the advantages of both architectures, maintaining detection sensitivity comparable to conventional cylindrical MOTs [1] while offering significantly improved performance. Our design maintains a similar detection limit to earlier grating-based MOTs [4] and features a capture range approximately ten times greater than that of the grating coil configuration in [3]. Furthermore, the trap volume is reduced to less than 1% of the area used by a standard MOT. This planar configuration not only minimizes optical and magnetic setups but also eliminates the need for a 3D magnetic gradient, rendering it ideal for applications in portable, miniaturized, and mass-producible quantum technologies. By utilizing the chain rule, we can calculate the gradient of the loss function regarding the parameters of a multi-objective loss specifically designed to steer MLP approximations toward valid solutions across the full space-time domain. Utilizing these gradients, we implement an automatic differentiation technique within gradient-based optimization frameworks to train MLPs that satisfy both differential equations and their boundary conditions. This approach, applied to solve Cauchy problems, ensures theoretical convergence to a solution as MLP capacity increases, provided the network capacity is sufficient for the training phase. Since the method depends solely on sample points, it extends naturally to scenarios where only noisy observations are available. In this context, our approach can be viewed as a data-driven framework for solving functional Cauchy problems, applicable even when the solution space is unknown. This represents another data-driven method for solving functional differential equations, applicable in situations where functional forms cannot be derived from other sources, such as PDE discovery. Because our method relies on sample points, it complements existing network-based approaches by effectively handling problems where the evaluation domain is difficult to define. Leveraging these findings, we establish a methodology and present computational data confirming that every ideal class in $\mathcal{O}$ is either Euclidean or pseudo-Euclidean with respect to a norm ideal. Additionally, we examine the relationship between pseudo-Euclidean algorithms and the extended continued fraction method proposed by Mordell for the case $d = 163$. Our computational analysis also provides direct proofs for two of Shen's conjectures. Furthermore, our results address one of Delorme's questions and facilitate a comparison with the work of Cullity and Mullen regarding norm–volume relations among pseudo-Euclidean ideal classes. Finally, we outline criteria that confirm lower bounds for the norms of non-Euclidean generators of these ideal classes. Some of these bounds are provided explicitly for the rings of integers of $k(1)$. Known results for cubic and larger-degree fields are also referenced. Abstract

Classical electron attachment (CEA) serves as a diagnostic tool for charge transfer dynamics occurring during ion-molecule reactions. This study presents CEA cross sections across various impact voltages for reactions involving water, methane, and methanol. The results indicate that the primary reaction pathway for ionized hydrocarbons is charge transfer from the incident ion to a neutral molecule, specifically hydrogen or water. The cross sections align reasonably well with a mechanism involving the collision of an outer-shell electron with the molecule, where the section ratio between two ions is approximately equivalent to the square of their outermost orbital radius ratio. The observed trends support a model in which charge transfer is governed by long-range Coulomb interactions between the incident ion and the neutral molecule, combined with a repulsive barrier arising from like-charge repulsion between the transferred electron and the neutral species.

The influence of a universal rescaling of momenta on quantization, manifesting as a deformation of the algebra of global shape operators, is explored. This phenomenon has already been validated experimentally in a cold-atom quantum gas. Within a theoretical framework, we demonstrate that these transformations constitute generalized quantum groups, a concept well-established in algebraic and statistical physics but previously unseen in quantum geometry. These findings offer a novel foundation for understanding quantum group symmetries. The approach is demonstrated through two solvable models: a particle on a circle and a particle on a plane featuring angular-dependent potentials.

We introduce a new class of quantum groups formed by deforming the algebra of globally defined Killing vector fields on a compact Lie group using a universally rescaled left-invariant Kähler form. These structures represent quantum symmetries in a broad sense. Their R-matrices are explicitly calculated for low-rank cases and derived generally using Hecke-algebra techniques. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding star products and show that these quantum groups are actually Poisson-Lie groups. We also establish the relevant Serre relations and raise questions regarding their Drinfel'd double. These findings have significant implications for the formulation of quantum group-symmetric quantum field theories. Specifically,

SU(6)/Sp(6)$ coset, wherein a $U(1)$ subgroup within $Sp(6)$ is interpreted as a family symmetry. This specific setup naturally generates three families of fermions through top terms, which also mediate interactions between the Standard Model and a "dark sector" consisting of additional gauge and Higgs fields. This dark sector can generate a small baryon asymmetry via leptogenesis and may offer explanations for dark matter and the circumgalactic medium. Additionally, we propose a future collider signature involving a vector boson resonance that couples to both Standard Model and non-Standard Model fields, potentially detectable by the High Luminosity LHC and future hadron colliders. The realization of three families relies on a 6-dimensional Higgs field, and the framework predicts its composite nature through a rich spectrum of heavy resonances. Given these complexities, we develop and validate a systematic approach employing the effective field theory formalism to construct the relevant operators. Finally, the methods described herein are applicable to various other coset models.

BigScience's 1.3-billion-parameter pretrained multilingual model, which initially supports 13 languages. This study examines the elements influencing the model's language adaptability and analyzes the trade-offs between computational expenses and anticipated performance. Our results indicate that the base model exhibits strong inherent capacity for language generalization. Furthermore, adding new languages requires minimal computation, whether through reusing the existing optimizer or implementing gradient accumulation with the original optimizer. After fine-tuning on in-domain data, the base model demonstrates competitive performance in language understanding against other big-transformers designed specifically for Korean and German. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the inclusion of additional languages while minimizing both costs and environmental impact. To support the research community, we will release the model and our findings.

The transformation of natural language processing by pretraining models like GPT-2 and BERT on vast corpora has sparked intense interest in enhancing language coverage. However, simply expanding training data or translating languages is financially and temporally prohibitive. An alternative strategy involves slightly adapting a pretrained model to new languages using a few paragraphs of text. This approach raises critical questions: which adaptation strategy yields the best results with the least computational effort, and which transfer learning techniques can be reused across multiple languages? Addressing these issues, we focus on two major underrepresented languages, Korean and German. We test several adaptation methods while keeping gradient updates to a minimum to limit computational costs. Our findings show that both XLNet and BERT achieve strong results on new languages after fine-tuning on just two articles. Additionally, using different optimizer learning rates for the head and body layers significantly boosts performance and result consistency. To share these insights and foster future research, our code and models will be made public. This study will help assess the multilingual adaptability of big-pretrained models and encourage the future expansion of their language support. Our code will be available at \url{https://github.com/SEOKYOUNG-KIM/NLLP2021-Multilingual-Pretrained-Models}.

have revealed circumstellar disks around protostars in the Ophiuchus region at an average resolution of 15 mas. By integrating these observations with archival Spitzer data, the study confirms a consistent two-phase structure across all samples: compact dust concentrations ranging from 15 to 63 mas and more extensive ionized gas distributions spanning on the order of 1000 mas. This newly identified disk population exhibits distinct evolutionary trends based on host star characteristics and the stage of collapse, aligning with a revised fragmentation model. Star formation within Ophiuchus appears gradual and continuous, with stars born within a narrow mass interval ($\sim$0.2 - 0.5 solar masses) displaying similar disk sizes and ages. Conversely, disks associated with stellar mass hosts are significantly smaller than those around brown dwarfs, supporting a brown dwarf formation mechanism distinct from standard disk accretion-induced core-collapsal models. Furthermore, disk sizes vary with the intensity of the collapse process: collapses producing bright methanol lines yield disks of 100 to 200 mas, whereas those with weak methanol signals have disks at least four times larger. Finally, the age distribution of disks with different associated components indicates that while dust disks and ionized gas appear simultaneously during stellar collapse, disks with bright maser emission are, on average, approximately ten times older than those without. These findings offer a novel perspective on the continuous process of star and disk formation in nearby star-forming regions. The complete dataset is accessible at http://www.ostrich.org.

While the kernel trick allows dimensionality reduction techniques to model greater non-linearity, there remains a scarcity of reproducible, open-source kernels, particularly for widely used like Independent Component Analysis (ICA). To address this, we extend the kernel's range and robustness across various distributions by integrating the robust kernel ('ar-K') developed by Mccutcheon et al. (2021) with Like ICA (fastICA) developed by Hyvarinen (2001). Our method is notably efficient, leveraging fastICA's superior computational efficiency, convergence speed, and stability compared to other FastICA (kernel) variants. We evaluate performance using two synthetic datasets and one real-world application, comparing our approach against fastICA (Gaussian kernel), biplot Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Independent Component Analysis (ICA), Kullback-Leibler Self Organizing Map (KLSOM), and Neighbourhood Component Analysis (NCA). Utilized for text feature extraction, the algorithm was tested on a dataset of 7,680 news articles categorized by political leaning and 35 additional features, followed by an Independent Set (IS) classification model. Feature extraction was performed using top 2,000 words (TF-IDF) and top 5,000 characters, with performance measured by Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Results indicate that m-ar-K-FastICA outperformed all comparison algorithms in NMI and MAE scores, achieving 0.5347 (NMI) and 0.3883 (MAE) for the text feature extraction task, thus validating its effectiveness. The code is accessible and reproducible at: github.com/Samarth1010/m-ar-K-FastICA. The method successfully extracts features for diverse data types, enhancing ICA's capacity to capture greater independence, which is critical for subsequent learning tasks. Given its robustness, convergence speed, and stability, this algorithm holds promise for applications including text feature extraction, text clustering, and independent learning. We anticipate it to be highly valuable for learning from unbalanced, mixed textual and numerical data (7-Corpus), facilitating better downstream prediction. The method is released under the MIT (Permission) license.

Specifically, we examine invariance principles, originally introduced by McElroy and Meyer, which connect a family of finite objects to a family of recursive objects. We demonstrate that every invariance principle can be derived from the comprehensiveness axiom, which states that for any structure $\mathcal{C}$ within the family and any recursive set $P$, there exists a morphism from $P$ to $\mathcal{C}$ such that all associated functions are themselves recursive. This result is straightforward, as each principle inherently implies comprehensiveness for an equivalent family. Building on this, we prove that logical comprehension is equivalent to invariance. Furthermore, we establish that any object belonging to a family satisfying an invariance principle is computable in polynomial time from any set that interprets within that object. By utilizing constraint relaxation techniques for non-convex optimization and adapting the standard cross-entropy loss function, we enforce posterior robustness against worst-case perturbations within $\epsilon$-balls surrounding input data points. We demonstrate how this framework integrates with existing methods for approximate inference in BNNs. Empirical results on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that our approach successfully trains certifiably robust models and improves uncertainty calibration. As the first method to directly train certifiable BNNs, our work supports their deployment in safety-critical applications by leveraging measure-theoretic uncertainty quantification. -19 pandemic triggered a surge in search queries for terms like "coronavirus" and "covid19." In response, Twitter launched a feature allowing users to tag their posts with the conversation starter "#COVID19," a mechanism known as conversation starters (CS). This study examines the impact of such CS activation on content quality by analyzing the proportion of health-related tweets versus those containing conspiracy theories immediately following the upgrade, and comparing them to historical data spanning 2017 to 2020. The results indicate that the introduction of #COVID19 as a CS increased health-related discourse while decreasing the frequency of conspiracy theories. Furthermore, a longitudinal analysis from March 2020 to March 2021 reveals a consistent decline in conspiracy theories on the platform, which correlates with the sustained use of conversation starters. These findings offer insights into designing CS mechanisms that promote beneficial user behaviors on social media. Beyond Twitter, the study discusses the broader implications of these findings for other social platforms, such as integrating conversation starters into Facebook news feeds to enhance overall platform quality. Ultimately, this research underscores the potential for platform designers to leverage conversation starters as a means of encouraging positive user interactions. To support this, we provide a link to the study's source code. By leveraging real-world data, this work demonstrates the value of empirical analysis in evaluating the effects of new platform features, ultimately aiding designers in making more informed decisions. This work was recognized with an Outstanding Paper Award at the 2022 European Conference on Information Systems (ECIS). Keywords: COVID-19, Conspiracy Theories, Conversation Starters, Twitter, Social Media.

A general framework for producing two jets in pairs in proton-proton collisions involving potential NP at the LHC is applied to top quark and diboson ($WW, ZZ, ZZ$) production and potential Higgs phenomena (Higgs boson production and potential Higgs triplet model) within the dijet channel. The analysis demonstrates that both experimental uncertainties and systematic errors—both negligible and non-negligible—can induce shifts in Higgs and diboson ratio predictions that mimic effects resembling Higgs and triplet model physics. Consequently, the paper concludes that Higgs and diboson ratio measurements in the dijet channel are unlikely to yield significant insights into Higgs triplet models or any similar scenario. Furthermore, it suggests that Higgs and diboson ratio measurements in the dijet environment may not be sufficient to establish a compelling case for excluding potential Higgs signals and could face obstacles in confirming or ruling out the Higgs triplet model. Finally, the study proposes that among all Higgs and diboson ratio measurements at the LHC, those in the dijet environment are likely to face the greatest challenges in constraining potential Higgs triplet models. excessive number of parameters often leads to over-training. This paper addresses the challenge of both efficient network design and robust feature extraction within a unified framework. O'Neil et al. previously introduced the Deep Multi-Task Learning (DMTL) approach, which simultaneously optimizes networks for robust feature extraction and low bit-width parameter quantization by treating quantization error as an additional optimization task. We extend this DMTL method in two significant ways: first, we generalize error bounding techniques from non-convex to convex programs, and second, we apply these bounds to construct the deep node graph of the optimization program, enabling automated and resource-aware network architecture design. Our results demonstrate that DMTL networks consistently outperform conventionally quantized models on image classification tasks. Furthermore, by varying quantization resources and robustness requirements, we successfully optimized and evaluated the performance of 2-bit to 6-bit networks. Notably, a 2-bit DMTL network matched the accuracy of a 6-bit unquantized network on CIFAR-10. Successfully generated and evaluated 3-bit unquantized networks, this work represents, to the best of our knowledge, the state-of-the-art in ultra-low-resource deep network modeling. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/azeeh-ooneil/DMTL.

the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. Ultimately, we aim to shed light on this often-neglected aspect and foster further research into the design and selection of effective classification losses.

However, defining the set of admissible boundary conditions for $\Gamma$ at a specific interface between two different media remains a challenging problem. This stands in contrast to the case for $\Gamma_0$, the grand potential, which captures only one-particle irreducible correlations. For $\Gamma_0$, a unique solution exists because the equilibrium density profile at the interface with a third body (a probe) is experimentally determinable. To address the analogous missing boundary condition issue for $\Gamma$, we propose a condition where the density profile is fixed to its bulk value at the interface. We demonstrate that this condition is compatible with a field-theoretic description of $\Gamma$ and can be translated into a constraint on the in situ potential of mean force. We further show that both the "in situ" in situ potential of mean force and the "equilibrium" in situ potential of mean force satisfy this constraint. Finally, we discuss the implications of this condition for the formulation of a density functional based on $\Gamma$. This density functional must utilize a class of boundary conditions at a substrate that are distinct from the partial density profiles at the interface measured in specific experimental scenarios. This requirement highlights a potential source of confusion and inconsistency in existing functionals derived from $\Gamma$. This new constraint may also offer fresh insights into the fundamental physics of interacting soft-matter particles assembled at interfaces. This study examines three such systems to identify structural biases inherent in their design and how these biases are amplified during the machine learning classification process. We introduce an interactive visualization tool that links individual worker predictions to the specific biases driving them, offering a new framework for detecting and analyzing bias within risk assessment systems. The insights gained from this tool will enable providers of electronic risk assessment systems to implement corrective measures, ultimately ensuring fairer safety evaluations for all workers. To support this research, we have released our dataset and code via the Useless Wiki at https://uselesswiki.org/. We invite the community to explore how these findings can promote greater transparency and equity in safety systems and encourage the development of methodologies to mitigate bias at both human and algorithmic levels. This tool not only aids in identifying bias but also serves as an educational resource for workers, inspectors, and managers to better understand the systems they use. Furthermore, we hope this approach encourages researchers to move beyond the binary good-versus-evil perspective of bias detection and to investigate design strategies that foster inclusive and equitable safety systems. We look forward to collaborating with safety system developers to deploy these tools in real-world settings and to engage with the broader community to advance the field of inclusive risk assessment design. We welcome questions and wish to establish a dialogue to inspire future research initiatives. Please visit our website for more information.

the most informative samples for human annotation. Concept selection is a prevalent approach within this framework, aiming to choose the most representative samples from unsupervised clustering. However, current methods often restrict selection to only the largest clusters and lack a strategy to verify cluster quality. We introduce valid concept selection, where representativeness within each cluster directly dictates sample selection. Its key innovation is an efficient algorithm capable of identifying samples across all clusters, not merely the largest ones. Valid concept selection is grounded in the assumption that clusters are concept homogeneous; therefore, the maximum cluster representativeness must exceed a specific threshold, known as the validity gap. This approach successfully recovers labeled examples from every cluster in synthetic datasets. Furthermore, we applied valid concept selection to a non-interactive setting for digit classification, demonstrating its effectiveness in selecting a minimal number of samples to reduce the overall labeling burden. By applying statistical physics methods to network analysis of song similarities across various feature spaces, we track the trajectory of this complex metric over time. Our findings indicate that while song similarity forms a single connected component throughout the examined period, the interconnected complexity of popular music has increased by approximately 50% between 1960 and 2010. This rise is linked to the increasing influence of computer-generated auto-tune effects and greater cross-cultural borrowing. Furthermore, we observe a decline in the two-hub structure of the network during this timeframe. These results are consistent with Marcuse's (1992) hypothesis from *The Aesthetic of Indifference*, which suggests a parallel growth in cultural complexity and indifference in Western culture over the past half-century. Additionally, we note a significant increase in popularity and listener interest in songs that are more distant in complexity space, corroborating our findings and offering a potential explanation for the observed growth in music consumption. These outcomes validate the application of statistical physics and complex network theories to cultural analysis and highlight the utility of employing similarity-based networks to model evolving complex systems. Finally, our work provides empirical support and precision to the concept of entropic value in art, demonstrating how aesthetic analysis can be rendered both quantitative and accessible through emerging interdisciplinary fields at the intersection of complex systems, physics, and the humanities. This research also seeks to offer a nuanced counter-perspective to the predictions of "The End of History and the Last Man" by Francis Fukuyama and "No Future" by William Gibson, which posited that cultural and artistic development would reach a plateau of maximal diversity.

by a sequence of random partitions $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, lt\}$, where $l \in \mathbb{N}$ is a parameter. At each step, a pair of elements is chosen uniformly and added to the partition if they differ in their bin-count modulo $d$ for a given $d \ge 2$; otherwise, the step is discarded. We establish that the proportion of bins, measured by cardinality, converges almost surely to a deterministic limit (which is $1/d$ when $d$ divides $l+1$) as $t \to \infty$. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic distribution of the number of partitions by cardinality under the scaling $1/\log t$. These results generalize Baryal and Tichy's primarily combinatorial approach, which assumed the selection of pairs at each step $[2]$. Specifically, we provide explicit formulas for both the exact distribution and the asymptotic distribution of the counts of partitions by cardinality. Furthermore, we combine these findings with Erd\H{o}s and R\'enyi's asymptotic result regarding the distribution of connected components in a random graph to generate two independent and identically distributed sequences of partitions, for which the latter determines whether two elements reside in the same bin. For this family of partitions, the limiting distribution of the counts by cardinality is also determined. In particular, we demonstrate that the normalized sum of partitions by cardinality converges in distribution to a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)$ with computable parameters, and that the covariance between the numbers of bins by cardinality converges to 0 if $d$ does not divide $l+1$ and to 1 if $d$ divides $l+1$. These findings extend and refine prior research, offering a more accurate approximation of the distribution for small values of $l$ and $t$. Notably, the infinite-volume limit of our primary process corresponds to a specific special case of the broader random partition family introduced by Trefler, which is derived from a broader random pair-addition process. This result enables the refinement of combinatorial estimates for specific partitions previously established by Baryal, P\'echou\'ek, and Tichy. By utilizing the Computational Ludics framework, we unify these two principles into a single condition termed the harmony condition. This reformulation elucidates two core intuitions: first, that the inversion and recovery principles are fundamentally one and the same; second, that formulating the criteria for valid logical constants becomes operational through an appropriate interaction strategy, specifically the polarisation strategy, rather than requiring a separate definition. Furthermore, we extend this approach to cover logical principles such as contraction and cut, and the meta-logical concepts of validity and inconsistency. Finally, we introduce the notion of polarisation in polarisation strategy as a precise characterization of interaction strategies that impose the harmony condition. The primary advantage of this framework over traditional proof-theoretic semantics lies in its constructive nature and its ability to handle logical principles like contraction and cut, as well as the invalidity of principles such as double negation elimination, in a uniform manner. Additionally, we demonstrate that the polarisation framework serves as a powerful tool for investigating the relationships between various concepts of validity across different schools of logic.

While this area has numerous applications in active learning and automated data labeling, there are also opportunities to leverage it for interactive reinforcement learning. In such scenarios, an agent must not only maximize its objective function but also adhere to constraints on the total number of interactions allowed. We introduce a sample-complexity-based framework for evaluating the efficiency of policy improvement methods within an interactive setting constrained by the sample budget. We prove that Supervised Policy Improvement, which fine-tunes a pre-trained policy using off-policy data, is the most efficient approach with the lowest sample complexity. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method is the only linear method capable of achieving O(1) sample complexity across all environments, a result that also holds in the online setting. Our findings indicate that methods relying solely on batch optimization are significantly less sample-efficient than those that incorporate online updates during deployment, even when the latter are restricted to a few additional steps beyond the offline sample set. Finally, we validate these theoretical results through experiments on both simple deterministic tasks and the MuJoco robotic simulation environment. Overall, this paper provides a theoretical analysis of sample efficiency in various proposed approaches to establish a foundation for future research in this domain. This note examines the impact of new physics in $\tau$ decays on B-factory observables that could be measured within the current data-taking period at B-factories. We identify the most significant $\tau$-decaying new physics contributions and calculate their sizes using hadronic form factors derived from B-meson decay observables. These form factors can be determined either through lattice QCD or from $B$-factory data in the specific kinematic regions of interest. Our findings indicate that a 1% relative uncertainty in these form factors is sufficient to resolve the new physics effects. Given that this precision aligns with expected form factor accuracies from either lattice QCD or B-factory experiments, we conclude that B-factory form factor precision is adequate to distinguish between the two possible origins of new physics in $\tau$ decays. Additionally, we provide several useful relations linking B-factory form factors to those in meson-to-meson transitions, which may serve as useful tools in other contexts. Finally, we discuss the relevance of our results to future $\tau$ factory proposals, such as CLIC, ILC, CEPC, and FCC-ee.

popular tabletop laboratory model for simulating mid-latitude atmospheric jet and wave dynamics. In this setup, air within a cylindrical channel between two coaxial cylinders (rotating together at a constant angular velocity $\varOmega$) is subject to an azimuthal temperature gradient. The hot inner inner-wall (at radius $r_1$) transfers heat to the cooler outer outer-wall (at radius $r_2$), an process influenced by the system's rotation. This configuration generates two vertical buoyancy forces: a positive force on the heated inner side driving upward motion, and a negative force on the cooled outer side inducing downward motion. The strength of these gradients is typically controlled by applying electrical heating films to the inner wall while cooling the outer wall via a Peltier element. The resulting flow instability is frequently expressed through planetary wave patterns, making the system valuable for testing numerical algorithms. However, the high nonlinearity of the equations of motion often makes it difficult to determine the precise flow state from pressure field measurements. To address this, we present an image-based image deconvolution (IBD) algorithm capable of deconvolving turbulent flow images to yield clearer results. When applied to laboratory images of the annulus flow, this method successfully reconstructs even heavily blurred images by inverting the azimuthal temperature gradient. Although the IBD algorithm does not produce a single unique solution, it reveals distinct characteristics of the turbulent flow that were previously obscured by excessive blurring. Although developed for the rotating annulus, the technique is broadly applicable to any turbulent flow exhibiting planetary wave structures. Finally, we demonstrate that the IBD algorithm complements, rather than replaces, traditional image analysis based on direct planetary wave counting. While traditional methods remain essential for assessing jet wave number and storm frequency, image deconvolution offers a novel capability to extract flow information from extremely blurred images previously considered unusable. Furthermore, it opens new avenues for applying machine learning to turbulence analysis. While current image analysis relies on clear images to directly count waves, deconvolution allows waves to be reconstructed from out-of-focus images. A convolution neural network could then be trained to identify and count these reconstructed waves, potentially determining the most probable wave number from a given set of blurred images. This approach could significantly aid in analyzing large-scale datasets, such as those collected over the entire year of a specific experiment. While beyond the scope of the current work, exploring this concept represents a promising direction for future research. Overall, the proposed image deconvolution algorithm could serve as a novel addition to the existing arsenal

This study models a specific device operating on an isotropic surface, featuring two identical four-legged figures linked by a rigid connector, where one figure acts as a motor and the other as a wheel. The figure-eight-shaped device is represented using Cartesian coordinates constrained by nonholonomic constraints, which are formulated as differential relations without associated integral constraints. Assuming the figure planes remain parallel to the isotropic surface during motion, these constraints can be reduced to a smaller system involving only the orientation angles of the planes and the position of the center of mass. This reduced system of constraints is non-integrable, indicating that the system is non-holonomic even though each individual constraint is integrable. The movable state space of this constrained system is accessed to analyze a specific artificial motor system, in which a time-dependent control torque is applied to the motor figure to generate unidirectional motion along the surface. This control strategy forces the motor into a rolling motion without slipping. It is demonstrated that the integral curves of a specific vector field, which is a linear combination of the vector fields associated with the nonholonomic constraints, point in the opposite direction to the asymptotic limit of the motor's positional integral curves under this control. This relationship between the local and global behaviors of the artificial motor is interpreted through a theorem applicable to constrained mechanical systems. This theorem establishes that for such a system, if a movable state space admits a reparametrization of the time axis such that it becomes accessible as a contact manifold with non-integrable constraints, then a specific set of necessary conditions must be met. Crucially, if any of these conditions are violated by the system, it guarantees that the system is holonomic, meaning all its constraints are integrable. This work contributes to the growing field of artificial molecular motors by providing a mathematical analysis of their properties and potential applications. Furthermore, it elucidates how the design of these organic-based devices influences their kinematic and dynamic behavior during motion. Finally, the paper provides a historical overview of the development of nonholonomic mechanics and its current status. Some results were previously presented at the XI Brazilian Congress on Mathematics in Belém, Pará, in 2019 [100].

This paper presents an additional decidability result concerning transducers that approximate one-way transducers within the origin semantics framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is decidable whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an origin-equivalent one-way transducer via resynchronization by a finite set of pairs. This finding contrasts sharply with standard semantics, where determining if a non-deterministic transducer is equivalent to a deterministic one is a notoriously hard problem. Our proof strategy relies on characterizing approximations of origin semantics through the lens of greatertree acceptance, thereby establishing a decision procedure for a broad category of transducers that recognize the language product of two context-free languages and possess a univariate greatertree acceptance index. Furthermore, we provide an independent proof that it is decidable whether the language recognized by a non-deterministic two-way finite automaton with a finite number of mistakes belongs to the class of context-free languages, and for which a corresponding "transducer with a finite number of mistakes" can be constructed to represent the original automaton. This resolves an open problem established in the context of origin semantics. Notably, our methodology is distinct from the standard approach based on Presburger arithmetic, which had previously been solved by Ochmanski. Our primary tool, the generation index, is also applicable in the standard setting, where it had never before been used to address the equivalence problem. Consequently, we demonstrate that checking whether the generation index of a non-deterministic two-way automaton accepting a context-free language is bounded by a constant is a decidable problem. This answer to the equivolume problem for context-free languages is achieved through a completely independent method, which also provides the product of two context-free languages with a linear generation index by constructing a one-way automaton and proving the linearity of its associated path acceptance index using semilinear set theory. first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of extensive study for nearly three decades due to its unique nature as a cool, isolated brown dwarf. Analyzed for the first time using modern state-of-the-art facilities and techniques, this paper elucidates the physical and chemical mechanisms driving its atmospheric evolution. Utilizing near-infrared spectra from the Gran Telescopio Canarias, we recently identified new emission lines in its spectrum, specifically those of Cs and Y. By combining these findings with existing data across multiple wavelengths, we modeled the most probable atmospheric conditions, determining that the object likely possesses a relatively "fugitive" (reducing) atmosphere. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a_f and non-equilibrium (shock-driven) chemistry is necessary to accurately explain these observations. Additionally, we identified a previously unknown mode of atmospheric activity in this object, characterized by an metal-line phase occurring between quiescence and a near-infrared stochastic storm, alongside a cooler mid-latitude belt compared to its hot zones, a configuration not previously seen in other brown dwarfs. The recent rapid brightening of GJ 229B in the infrared since 2020 suggests this event represents a stochastic storm, a phenomenon not yet documented in other brown dwarfs, and we provide evidence for the presence of chaotic surface spots during this period. Finally, we show that the object's current luminosity cannot be accounted for by heating from internal processes, stellar flares, or accretion. These results offer new insights into the current and past activity of the system, opening a new field of "brown dwarf astroseismology" and suggesting the possibility of similar phenomena in other brown dwarfs and gas giant exoplanets. This study marks a novel approach in the observational analysis of gas giant exoplanets. A companion article explicitly investigates the cause and mechanism of this phenomenon.

However, the algorithm governing these auctions is often opaque to market participants, raising concerns about transparency and the alignment of outcomes with individual rationality. This note provides a formal analysis of double-sided auctions by examining their connection to general equilibrium theory through the lenses of existence, uniqueness, and incentive compatibility. Our findings reveal a striking contrast between single and double-sided auctions: while the unique general equilibrium in a standard auction is known to be incentive compatible, this is not the case for double-sided auctions. Specifically, we identify that when sellers face a fixed quantity constraint, the unique general equilibrium fails to incentivize bidders to report their true valuations. Under this modification, we prove that the unique general equilibrium is incentive compatible for all agents. Furthermore, by leveraging properties of general equilibria, we establish a sequence of auctions whose limiting outcome converges to a unique general equilibrium with incentive compatibility, without altering the auction rules for price or quantity allocation to the house. Finally, an epsilon-based welfare analysis confirms that both existence and uniqueness hold for this model. addresses three modeling challenges: (i) system identification, (ii) dimensionality reduction, and (iii system compression. These challenges are frequently addressed in isolation. This work unifies these approaches to system compression by introducing system-sparse neural networks (SSNNs). An SSNN is a feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) composed of a cascade of operators: (SS) state, (sp) sparse coding, and (N) nonlinear, designed such that its input-output (I/O) characteristics align with the fundamental properties of the target dynamical system. The approach is validated on three key benchmarks: system identification, dimensionality reduction, and system compression. Notably, we demonstrate that SSNNs can be constructed as a strict subset of the input-output equivalence class containing all feed-forward Anns that match the input-output behavior of the target dynamical system. Furthermore, we show that SSNNs can be derived as a strict subset of the latent space unitary group (UG) containing all linear transformations of the state space. Finally, we establish that SSNNs can be formed as a strict subset of the latent space Lie group containing all deformations of the state space. Thus, SSNNs serve as a canonical structure for data-driven modeling of dynamical systems, effectively integrating input-output equivalence, Lie group, and latent space geometry concepts. This framework is applicable to time series, experimental data, and any signal representing a dynamical system. Furthermore, SSNNs are entry-level accessible, can be implemented as a drop-in replacement for any standard feed-forward ANN, and are implemented in the DYNAMO Python toolbox, which also includes a collection of related sparsity-based structures and models. The SSNN structure is entry-level accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10021260 and is published at https://doi.org/10.1093/imanum/drab105. The DYNAMO Python toolbox is published at https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119619922. Our findings indicate that SSNNs provide a more efficient, interpretable, and informative structure than any standard feed-forward ANN for dynamical system modeling. The findings encompass a new fixed-parameter algorithm based on the count of sources, an XP-algorithm defined by treewidth, and another fixed-parameter algorithm utilizing treedepth. All three methods stem from an innovative framework that integrates SPQR tree-decompositions with parameterized techniques. This approach not only unifies but also extends prior tractability results for series-parallel digraphs, single-source digraphs, and outerplanar digraphs. Out of 22 identified cases where parameters include treewidth, pathwidth, or treedepth, this work addresses 10, while three additional papers cover the remaining instances. Out of 6 cases involving treedepth, this study resolves 4.

We also examine the related non-planar upward planar linkage problem, for which we provide multiple parameterized algorithms. In this context, we establish that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of sources, pathwidth, or treewidth, with the last two being the first such fixed-parameter algorithms identified. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the problem is XP-complete with respect to treewidth, and we present upper and lower bounds for algorithmic complexity based on chordal deletion parameters. Finally, we discuss additional parameterized algorithms for other variants of the problem. This research extends our earlier work published in the 37th International Colloquium on Automata, Languages, and Programming (ICALP), which was part of the 44th Symposium on the Theory of Computing Connection (2010).

Question: Does this work address the issue of whether a directed acyclic graph can be rendered planar in an upward manner? Answer: Yes.

Limitations: While our results are significant for fixed-parameter algorithms, they are less so for XP-algorithms, as the upper bound of O(n^{f(k)}\cdot k^{f'(k)}) is not tight. \indent\textbf{1.}--Introduction

\medskip

The study of pattern formation, whether chemical, biological, or physical, has been significantly advanced by the analysis of dynamical systems on spatially structured domains. This paper contributes to this field by investigating the conditions under which spatial patterns spontaneously arise from the coupling of differential equations representing local dynamics, which are then integrated into a partial differential equation system incorporating integral interaction terms or diffusion operators. Specifically, we examine how the entanglement structure of Fock states, which live in a tensor product space $\mathcal{H}_N\otimes\mathcal{H}_F$, evolves under dynamics characterized by an infinite-dimensional matrix product operator (MPO). This description relies on the underlying symmetry algebra's Casimir operators. To quantify such properties, we introduce a novel method using Schur vectors to characterize the state's structure within the Schur-Weyl double symmetry framework. Our findings demonstrate that these states maintain coherence across various quantum dimensions determined by the system's particle content, while also explicitly detailing how the dimensions of Schur-Weyl representation spaces scale with system size. Furthermore, these states can be constructed from initially product states with trivial correlations, even when the governing dynamics lack Hamiltonian symmetry. Finally, our approach successfully captures dynamics for operators that break symmetry down to a one-dimensional stabilizer subgroup. These theoretical predictions are supported by numerical validations for $su(1,1)$ and $su(2)$ algebras. Notably, cases involving non-hamiltonian symmetry dynamics show evidence of both operator and volume growth, which may have significant implications for quantum many-body problems and high-energy physics models. A key representative of this class involves dynamics generated by an MPO that decomposes a symmetry algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ into a one-dimensional subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$. In this context, the problem of operator growth transforms from a complex infinite-dimensional task into a manageable finite-dimensional character representation problem relative to $\mathfrak{h}$. This simplification is particularly relevant for modeling string worldsheet dynamics in high-energy physics, where worldsheet symmetry algebras are frequently broken to a U(1) isometry corresponding to movement along the string worldsheet. These findings suggest the ability to efficiently predict operator growth for strings with a conserved winding number around a circle. Additionally, our methods open new avenues for calculating complexity measures for states with a specific hierarchy of tensor product decompositions, where the remaining symmetry algebra acts diagonally. Among these, topological semimetals have garnered significant attention due to their rich mathematical foundations and diverse physical manifestations. This work introduces a method for calculating the Chern number of closed loops within the non-Hermitian band structure of topological semimetals, derived from the general theory of non-Hermitian winding numbers. Using the two-dimensional Bergholz model as a representative case, we demonstrate that loops of exceptional points (EPs) and non-Hermitian Dirac points give rise to distinct topological regimes. These regimes are characterized by unique values of the Chern number, which can be determined via the chemical potential, leading to rich phase diagrams. Furthermore, we show that phase transitions between regimes are driven by the emergence or collision of EPs and non-Hermitian Dirac points. Notably, a non-holomorphic deformation of the Hermitian Bergholz model results in a phase transition where both the Chern number and winding number are zero, accompanied by the appearance of a line of EPs in the band structure. Finally, we investigate the dynamics of Bloch electrons in non-holomorphic non-Hermitian topological semimetams, revealing topological polarization and current anomalies that provide clear signatures for experimentally identifying topological regimes in non-Hermitian systems. Our findings offer a foundation for classifying non-Hermitian topological semimetals and may aid in the discovery of topological semimetals in real-world material systems. Additionally, these results are expected to be applicable to other non-Hermitian topological systems.

Previously, Foss and Schalkwijk (2013) derived an exact formula for the feedback capacity of a discrete memoryless FSC with a fixed source distribution. This inquiry arises from an interest in the fundamental connection between signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the complexity of a channel that achieves a specific capacity value at that SNR. # 1. Deriving Darcy's Laws

Although various derivations of groundwater flow equations exist, I find the physical argument most compelling for my purpose here. I will sketch my preferred argument, which derives the vertically averaged mass conservation equation by applying Darcy's Law to the vertically averaged momentum equation. This approach relies on several simplifications and assumptions, some of which are explicitly stated in the following paragraph and others which are not. An assumption is required when a term is negligible compared to others in the momentum equation, a determination that can only be made after estimating the relative magnitudes of the terms. Given that groundwater flow is slow, I will examine the order of magnitude of each term in the momentum equation. First, let $U$ represent the characteristic speed of groundwater flow and $L$ the characteristic horizontal length scale. I will argue that the time derivative is of order $U^{-1}U = 1$, the pressure gradient term is of order $U/L U = U/L$, and the viscous term is of order $U/L L = U/L$. Since the time derivative order does not depend on the length scale, it cannot be ignored in the limit of large $L$. The pressure gradient term represents the order of magnitude relative to the viscous term, a comparison that depends on the ratio of horizontal to vertical length scales. Assuming the vertical scale is much smaller than the horizontal scale ($L/l \gg 1$), the viscous term dominates the momentum equation at large $L$. Consequently, I will show that the momentum equation reduces to hydrostatic balance at large $L$. Finally, I will apply the hydrostatic balance approximation to derive the vertically averaged momentum equation.

\section{Introduction}

As one of the most prominent frameworks in machine learning, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have garnered extensive research interest and industrial application over recent years. By effectively capturing both node representations and their local neighborhood relationships, GNNs have proven highly effective in tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and link classification.

Despite their success, the performance of GNNs is intimately tied to the degree of node and neighborhood aggregation. Excessive aggregation can lead to the over-smoothing problem. Specifically, when a GNN performs too many aggregation operations, node representations become too similar, rendering their neighborhood distinctions indistinguishable. Consequently, during the final classification phase, the model is unable to differentiate between nodes, which diminishes the network's discriminative capacity.

First observed in spectral GNNs like GCNs \cite{Kipf17}, over-smoothing has subsequently been documented in other GNN architectures \cite{wu2020b, li2019, you2019, ke2020, zhou2020, zeng2019, zeng2020, zeng2021, zeng2021icml, zeng2021t, zeng2021cmk, zeng2021cm}. This issue manifests in two primary ways. Quantitatively, node representations become nearly identical, causing the gradient variance to decline as training progresses. Qualitatively, the loss landscape transitions from convex to non-convex, resulting in an increase in test loss despite a continuous decrease in training loss. Driven by over-smoothing, these changes degrade the network's performance.

In this paper, we generalize the concept of a statistical model within the framework introduced in [DvDS18] and further develop the theory of statistical experiments as defined by Van Dorp and the second author in [vdDS20]. Following standard practice, we adopt the term "statistical model" for a collection of probability measures on a single sample space, while a "statistical experiment" refers to the same data representation utilizing observable random variables instead. We demonstrate that both statistical models and statistical experiments can be modeled as morphisms between appropriate C*-algebras. A central result is that, up to isomorphism, a statistical model is completely determined by the corresponding statistical experiment. This finding is demonstrated through the existence of a one-to-one correspondence between state spaces of appropriate C*-subalgebras and the states of the underlying C*-algebra of physical observables. This subgroup is closed and has the same cardinality as the original state space. Additionally, we finalize the investigation into when a statistical model can be simulated via a quantum measurement, using the language of C*-algebras and their representations. In this context, a quantum simulation is possible if and only if there exists a morphism between the corresponding abstract C*-subalgebras that maps the state of the quantum system in the quantum system to the state in the quantum measurement. Finally, we establish that up to isomorphism, a statistical model is equivalent to a quantum measurement if and only if the representing C*-algebras are unitarily equivalent. (This work is based in part on [vdDS20]).

This research constitutes the first dedicated effort to use data-driven nonlocal models for representing the transmission of the novel coronavirus in a specific nation, serving as a new reference point for modeling and simulating the disease's spread across various countries. The proposed model is operations research-friendly, readily applicable by public health officials to test different scenarios by adjusting model parameters. This work, which constitutes the first dedicated study on the topic, is expected to contribute to the effective control of novel coronavirus transmission. The proposed model is data-driven, derived from fitting a specific country's transmission data to a NND equation. This demonstrates that novel entities may exhibit both local and nonlocal diffusion behaviors. Given that other countries' transmission patterns often align more closely with those of the reference country, the temporal and spatial nonlocal diffusion characteristics observed in the reference country can be expected to occur in most other regions.

We then provide a fast computational algorithm based on the Fourier transform, delivering computational efficiency with associated error estimates. Following this, we offer a quick sensitivity analysis of the model's parameters, $\sigma$ and $\beta$.
