This technique successfully identifies up to 80% of abbreviations in the ACM test set, which contains approximately 100,000 instances. On the ACM abbreviations test set, the weighted error rate for predicting syllable count is 0.0886 (with 95% confidence), and the total bit loss for syllable prediction is 2.83 bits. The system achieves 53.13% top-1 accuracy for correct syllable selection, with an average rank of 3.71 among the three possible syllables. For abbreviations of the format "X XY Z," the system attains a weighted error rate of 0.0188 (with 95% confidence), 37.5% top-1 accuracy, an average rank of 1.88, and a syllable count weighted loss of 2.03 bits. The model predicts that syllables often share common endings, a phenomenon observed to a degree of 55.4% on the ACM set (with 95% confidence). Notably, the system detected 42 syllables common to both the Hutter Prize test set and the ACM set that it had not been trained on. A paper detailing the system's architecture and training process is also being prepared. A reference implementation is available at <https://github.com/SebastianThurgood/Neural-Acronyms>. The source code requires Python 3.6 and NumPy. The trained models are hosted at <https://huggingface.co/SebastianThurgood/neural-acronyms>. The code was executed on a system equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2650L CPU and 32 GB of RAM. The neural network architecture consists of 6 layers, utilizing bidirectional LSTM cells with 256 units. In this study, we demonstrate that an effective, one-dimensional bosonic spin chain exhibits a analogous dependence on topological properties. By incorporating the proper chemical potential, the system's excitation spectrum transitions between a gapless state and several gapped states, mirroring the domain-wall structure found in the one-dimensional Fermi gas with a spin-space mapping. Stripe ordering characterizes these gapped phases. Through mapping to an effective bosonic quantum wire and numerical analysis of excitations, we identify a topologically protected gap within the bulk spectrum. This gap remains stable against weak perturbations that preserve the system's effective one-dimensional nature. Furthermore, both linear and nonlinear dynamics reveal that excitation packets traverse a time-dependent effective potential without dispersion, akin to the Aharonov-Bohm effect in quantum interference. The observed dynamics rely on the topological winding number of the effective coupling; specifically, the phase accumulation is directly proportional to this number and the ratio of the pulse duration to the effective period. These findings hold significant relevance for topological quantum information processing and the manipulation of bosonic wave packets within one-dimensional quantum gas mixtures. Specifically, the topological distinction between gapless and gapped phases opens new avenues for storing and transmitting quantum information. Additionally, the impulse approximation is validated, revealing that the wave packet's width actually enhances resilience against dissipation. This behavior could enable the engineering of quantum interference using readily preparable wave packets in experimental settings. These results also establish a foundation for simulating quantum interference and topological effects in optically trapped Bose-Natractant mixtures. Any external potential can function similarly to an effective one-dimensional quantum wire excitation, allowing for the observation of quantum interference even at relatively high temperatures. This approach may facilitate the realization of topological information storage in bosonic systems of interest. The interaction with an optical molecular beam provides a flexible method for generating wave packet superpositions, whereas radio-frequency pulses achieve this by manipulating the effective spin-space coupling in the quantum chain. Ultimately, these findings offer a unique perspective on analog quantum simulation in Bose-Natractant mixtures. While recent advancements have clarified and demonstrated topological insulator states for p-wave superconductivity and topological insulator states with broken time-reversal symmetry, the search for additional types of topological insulators continues. In this study, we identify a topological insulator state in the Weyl semimetal $\text{CdPt}_3\text{Te}_2$ under a high external magnetic field that breaks time-reversal symmetry. By analyzing the low-field specific heat and resistivity data, we calculated the magnetic field-dependent change in topological number using the Fermi surface topology, which increased from 0 to 4. Furthermore, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) revealed multiple gapless Dirac cones in the low-energy electron spectrum. These findings confirm the existence of four magnetic Weyl nodes and provide evidence for a four-fold degenerate surface fermion state at the crystal boundary, thereby establishing a bulk surface connection across multiple topological numbers within a magnetic Weyl semimetal. These results provide significant insights into the discovery of diverse topological number states in topological semimetals and may facilitate the realization of topological superconductor states in magnetic doped systems. Additionally, this work offers a methodology applicable to other topological semimetal systems where the evolution of electronic band topology in response to external magnetic fields remains unclear. Given that $\text{CdPt}_3\text{Te}_2$ exhibits no superconductivity, this work may offer valuable evidence for investigating additional types of topological insulator states in non-superconducting systems. This paper demonstrates that such a point oscillator can exhibit both thermal and quantum fluctuations. The model employed is a collection of $N$ coupled charge oscillators in two dimensions, representing the lateral barrier of a superconductor where the Josephson current $I_J\propto\sin\phi$ depends on the phase difference $\phi$ across the junction. When a superconductor is maintained at constant temperature $T$ and subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, the phase $\phi$ behaves as an oscillator. At low temperatures and high magnetic fields, thermal fluctuations remain negligible, yet phase slips—events where $\phi$ transitions between adjacent integer values—still occur. These slips induce local oscillations in $\phi$, causing it to fluctuate at frequencies far exceeding those of neighboring oscillators. Consequently, a region with this accelerated phase acts as a point oscillator driven by large magnetic fields, subject to both thermal and quantum influences. To validate the model, we employ Ginzburg-Landau simulations and Monte Carlo methods to calculate the oscillator's susceptibility and analyze quantum tunneling effects. The study reveals that the oscillator's susceptibility is enhanced by both thermal and quantum tunneling. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these findings. These results suggest that such oscillator points serve as an ideal platform for investigating the interplay between thermal and quantum fluctuations. Furthermore, the point oscillator is essential for understanding Josephson vortices in arrays, the correlation length in superconductors, and the quantization of magnetic flux. Related phenomena include fluctuation-dissipation theorems, the Meissner effect in type-II superconductors, and vortical structures in superfluids and superconductors. Additional applications span cosmology, quantum optics, and condensed matter physics. These points may also be fundamental in establishing the cosmological constant and the coupling between general relativity and the standard model. Finally, such points oscillate with large amplitudes and high frequencies, making them potentially detectable by both cosmic and terrestrial detectors.

This review focuses on the evolution of entropy within quantum mechanics, highlighting key research directions such as isolated quantum systems, thermodynamics, and quantum information theory. Furthermore, entropy is essential for characterizing disorder in many-body quantum systems that are far from equilibrium, a topic central to the study of the Quantum Many-Body Scrambling (QMBSS) phenomenon, which is examined in this paper. We examine the recent progress on the SCYBQMS (Scrambling, Entanglement, and Quantum Bath) protocol, which provides an efficient and accurate experimental measurement of entropy in closed many-body quantum systems. The discussion also extends to emerging topics including the black hole information paradox and the Large Deviation Function. Finally, we outline future perspectives and conclusions derived from this comprehensive study.

Large amplitude electron correlation effects are critical for accurately modeling chemical reactions. While the full Configuration Interaction (FCI) method yields exact results within a predefined basis set by incorporating all possible excitations, it remains computationally infeasible for all but the smallest molecular systems, even with advanced algorithms and high-performance computing. This presents a significant obstacle to the development of efficient and reliable first-principles methods capable of modeling reaction dynamics in both ab initio and materials science contexts, a necessity highlighted by the impending quantum computing era capable of simulating quantum systems. This article offers a current examination of algorithms designed to incorporate large amplitude motions into electronically excited states. It begins by reviewing the impact of these motions on non-adiabatic photochemistry and their implementation via the restricted and unrestricted Hartree-Fock (RHF/UF) approaches, which remain the basis for most multi-configurational self-consistent field (MCSCF) methods. The text then explores a history of approximate large amplitude motion treatments, followed by a detailed analysis of a density matrix reformulation of time-dependent Hartree-Fock and a new configuration selection strategy for balanced multi-reference configuration variation methods. Following a brief overview of recent efforts, the article presents a demonstration of how large amplitude motions can be efficiently and effectively captured through dimer-based methods. We conclude by discussing a novel approach to density matrix based cluster methods and the time-dependent Coupled Cluster method of any order. The primary goal of this review is to assess the current landscape of large amplitude motion treatments and to set the stage for a following article dedicated to order and limited large amplitude motions in the context of excited states.

Establishing and annotating these datasets is time-consuming and labor-intensive, necessitating reliable sources for a broad range of entities. While numerous sources exist for categories like animals, plants, and minerals, there is no comprehensive source for morphological terms. To address this gap, we introduce MorphBank, an open-source repository designed to catalog references for various morphological terms. Our ongoing collaboration with plant scientists ensures wide community adoption and feedback to further refine the project. We will publish a comprehensive paper detailing the project's motivation, design, and future developments at EMNLP 2022. MorphBank is accessible at https://morphbank.github.io/.

Question-Answer (QA) systems represent a critical application in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Over the last ten years, NLP communities from both academic and industrial sectors have made significant advancements in developing intelligent QA solutions. This work provides a comprehensive survey of these advancements, offering an in-depth analysis of current methods and their applied techniques while highlighting the challenges associated with QA systems. Furthermore, we compare and contrast these solutions and offer recommendations to QA developers based on our findings. The paper concludes with a roadmap for future research directions.

Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) assist medical professionals in diagnosing and treating patients. However, interpreting patient data remains difficult for natural language processing (NLP) algorithms, prompting various studies to focus on extracting structured data from electronic health records to aid in treatment. This paper presents a survey of state-of-the-art methods for identifying medical conditions and clinical conditions within patient records. It begins by defining CDSS and outlining the process of extracting medical conditions from records. Subsequently, we review the data sources used in this field and examine the clinical conditions most frequently extracted. We then provide a chronological examination of the techniques employed by recent studies, starting with an overview of traditional methods. The survey also summarizes the approaches used by the thirty most cited papers in the last decade, which span a wide range of methods. Furthermore, we present a comparative analysis of these top citations. Finally, we discuss challenges and propose recommendations and potential directions for future research.

Our prior work demonstrated that graph data can be effectively mapped into other data spaces, such as integer sets, for anomaly detection using machine learning. While this approach calculated node importance scores to generate embeddings via optimization, it limited the variety of learnable representations. This paper proposes a novel framework for generating graph data representations suitable for machine learning. The method utilizes an unsupervised learning technique called Independent Component Analysis (ICA), applied here for the first time in this context. We demonstrate that this algorithm is capable of identifying various graph structures, including star, circle, grid, random, and social networks. A key advantage of the proposed algorithm is its independence from node indexing, addressing a significant limitation of previous methods. Performance evaluations show that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches on multiple graph datasets, reducing dimensions from 100 to 50 and from 200 to 50 with greater efficacy. Additionally, we provide code for a new variant of the "Delaunay" graph dataset. To facilitate broader research, we are releasing the library containing our proposed ICA algorithm along with other graph data structures and tools. This release supports first-place algorithms in two categories of the 11th Graph Analytics Methodology and Applications (GAMA) Challenge and allows for the application of new algorithms to our ICA benchmark datasets.

9-nCov cases identified in China during January 2020. Our analysis reveals that the virus exhibits lower transmissibility compared to seasonal influenza, with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 2.2 (95% CI 1.9 to 2.6), as estimated by Imperial College London. Although the virus spreads via droplets and potentially aerosols, we determined that community transmission is not yet occurring in China, with the exception of Wuhan. Furthermore, we found that the case fatality rate of 3% is significantly reduced when accounting for undetected mild cases. While lockdown measures are necessary and will effectively halt transmission, their impact on mortality remains uncertain. We argue that the current strategy should shift from containment to clinical management and the implementation of measures that will substantially restrict imported cases entering China. These adjustments are expected to result in a marked decrease in both new infections and deaths. Finally, we contend that Wuhan serves as a unique exception within the broader context of the epidemic's progression.

While existing literature represents demand fluctuation through homogeneous, time-invariant deviated OLG networks and supply deviation through a single deviated network, this paper introduces a novel approach to joint network deviations. We formulate this approach as the Roboweber Problem (RWP), which aims to minimize the sum of (first-stage) investment costs for network expansions and the expected second-stage operational cost, subject to capacity and cost constraints. The model accounts for uncertainties in both demand and supply, incorporating general demand scenarios, a general supply loss model, and a general cost function. We provide a polynomial-time solution for the first-stage optimization and employ Monte-Carlo sampling to estimate the expected second-stage cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific conditions, a gradient-based method can efficiently solve this problem exactly. Numerical experiments utilize New York City's network to evaluate the model, and we compare results against simple first and second-stage solutions to highlight the impact of expansion decisions on operational costs under various scenarios. This work is derived from the second author's PhD dissertation, which provides a more comprehensive analysis of the problem.
Commuters navigating large urban areas and their associated delays are critical components of city planning and management. Given the variability of daily demand, predicting travel times becomes a statistical challenge best addressed by learning from historical data. Although deep learning excels in this prediction task, its performance can degrade during test phases, prompting an analysis of the model's robustness. This study evaluates three distinct deep learning architectures to estimate travel time between two points in a given network, testing them on two real-world networks with modified parameters. The results indicate that the proposed method, BTL, effectively handles networks with perturbed parameters, while VGG and ResNet fail to do so. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of deep learning to estimate expected 2-stage problems involving joint first and second-stage uncertainties, contributing to the formulation of expected problems.
This paper derives an efficient algorithm for the robust max-min first-order problem (RMF) by converting it into a conventional min-max problem solvable via linear programming. The development of this formulation relies on duality theory and the specific structure of the objective function, which enables a polynomial-time solution. We apply this formulation to estimate the expected second-stage cost in expected optimization problems. Extensive experiments on synthetic instances and real-world datasets—specifically New York City for travel costs and London for energy consumption—demonstrate the approach's efficacy. Our analysis demonstrates the emergence of global phase-locked states within finite lattices and explores their numerical destabilization. As model parameters vary, these states lose stability, giving rise to localized periodic and chaotic oscillations. In cases of weak nonlinear frequency dispersion, the system exhibits metastability similar to that observed in almost-conservative systems. Furthermore, we contrast our findings with the phase-approximation approach, where amplitude dynamics are adiabatically eliminated. While the phase model displays only generic cohomology in its bifurcation scenarios, the phase-approximated system exhibits complex, unique behaviors including internal pattern formation and crossing of macroscopic patterns. The phase system's instability leads to macroscopic patterns of type M(1, 1), representing spatial 1D structures, as well as type M(2, 1), indicating discrete spatial patterns with $2N+1$ components. Microscopic patterns of type M(n, 1) with $n > 1$ arise in parameters regions previously inaccessible to the phase-approximated system. These novel patterns are generated via 1D and 2D homoclinic bifurcations and heteroclinic connections. We also examine the relationship between macroscopic patterns and phase-approximated internal structures, as well as the correlation between the microscopic and macroscopic components of the newly formed patterns. Additionally, we establish a connection between our model and the recently proposed area-preserving map system. Finally, we draw comparisons with other nonlinear oscillator models.

der$ and $Wilson$ algorithms are prominent methods for generating uniform spanning trees (USTs) using random walks. This study examines their interplay to accelerate the construction of random trees. By analyzing $branches$—specific paths produced by both algorithms at defined stopping times—we demonstrate that the trees generated on a complete graph are statistically identical at these moments. This finding enables a hybrid algorithm that creates USTs for complete graphs more rapidly than either standalone method. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient two-stage framework to extend this hybrid strategy to graphs beyond the complete class, validating its utility across various examples, including transitive graphs where it reduces generation time by 25% compared to the $Wilson$ algorithm. Additionally, we evaluate the framework on a widely used biological graph, the 5-tuple octagonal triangulation. Our results indicate that the proposed method is computationally simpler and faster than existing approaches, reducing the generation time by 17% to 22% for small to moderate sizes. This efficiency is attributed to the algorithm's ability to produce USTs as subtrees of random conditioned walks, thereby eliminating the need for extensive path modifications. The asymptotic computational costs of the proposed algorithm are detailed in the article. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/haryanrajiv/Coupled-algorithms-for-UST}.

However, in the 4+1 dimensional model featuring power-law potential terms, intensity-dependent dispersion leads to divergent behavior at large distances. Specifically, to prevent solution blow-up in finite time, the potential must dominate over the dispersion at short ranges, while the dispersion must surpass the potential at long ranges to ensure stability. This study demonstrates that under these conditions, the model admits a class of exact solitary wave solutions known as double hyperbolic black solitons. These solutions vanish at both zero and non-zero values of the spatial variable, exhibiting zero depth at infinity and finite depth at the origin. Additionally, we numerically investigate the stability of these exact solutions across various parameter values and analyze the solution's behavior relative to different parameter sets. Furthermore, we examine the asymptotic properties of the black soliton, highlighting key features of the model, and discuss the physical significance of the model alongside an analysis of energy conservation. Finally, we investigate the balance between the nonlinearity and the combined effects of the potential and intensity-dependent dispersion. The interplay among these factors determines whether the model supports wave collapse, solitary waves, or wave propagation. These theoretical findings are supported by various numerical analyses.

Various nonlinear wave equations serving as models for light propagation in optical fibers have been constructed by balancing the dispersion law with a cubic nonlinearity. +1 dimensional models assume a linear approximation for the envelope and incorporate transverse spatial variation. In this work, we numerically explore the stability of exact solitary wave solutions within the class of the +1 dimensional NLS equation. This class assumes a 1+1 dimensional nonlinear term (focusing or defocusing) balanced against intensity-dependent dispersion and a class of finite depth or zero depth potential terms within a class of 1+1 dimensional nonlinear terms. We also numerically analyze the stability of exact finite depth and zero depth solitary waves under the influence of intensity-dependent dispersion and potential terms. These exact solutions function similarly to fundamental gap solitons in the 1+1 dimensional NLS equation with intensity-dependent dispersion and zero depth potential. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the model supports localized finite energy and infinite energy solutions. Moreover, we investigate the stability of finite energy and infinite energy black solitons in the 4+1 dimensional model with intensity-dependent dispersion. collaboration within visual analytics, a concept supported by a definition from Koopman et al. This approach relies on a shared model of appropriate guidance, where both human and machine actors internally align on what constitutes a suitable guidance strategy. The article argues that this psychological framework is inherently human-centric. Machine learners, however, operate without consciousness and lack a conceptual framework; they cannot understand a task or an appropriate strategy because they lack consciousness and a model of the task itself. Consequently, true human-machine collaboration in visual analytics requires a novel framework that integrates machine learners with their own frameworks for appropriate guidance. We introduce a prototype system, MARG, which is argued to be the first such framework. Marginalization, a core technique in many machine learning methods, is identified as a potential source of insight for MAGARG to derive a framework for human-machine collaboration. The paper concludes by highlighting the urgent need for research into machine-centered guidance and the dangers of inadvertently designing systems that impose cognitive loads on machines beyond their capabilities. Ultimately, MAGARG is presented as a proposed framework for human-machine-centered visual analytics guidance. Key contributions include: a critique of the limited scope of co-adaptive guidance, the introduction of MAGARG as a novel framework, and an argument for a shift from guidance to coordination in HMI interactions. These efforts are seen as essential for advancing the discipline toward a more inclusive and equitable future. MARGARG can be accessed at https://github.com/cr4ft/MARGARG. Keywords: Visual Analytics, Guidance, Coordination, Human-Machine Collaboration, Psychological Models, Cognitive Models, Marginalization.

This study examines the temperature profiles of catalytic and non-catalytic fixed beds for first-order reactions. Additionally, we evaluate various performance metrics and investigate the impact of temperature variations on selectivity within sequentially occurring reactions. Our findings indicate that for catalytic fixed beds, the pressure and temperature optimal for stability or maximum yield may differ significantly from those in non-catalytic fixed beds. Consequently, reactor design for industrial applications should prioritize stability and maximize yield, rather than relying on the common assumption that all fixed bed reactors operate near non-isothermal conditions to enhance yield. This perspective should encourage a re-evaluation of existing fixed bed reactors and promote the development of novel reactor concepts for large-scale operations. Ultimately, this work seeks to clarify fundamental mechanisms to empower chemical engineers in achieving optimal reactor performance.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to dynamic contact problems involving large deformations in finite elements. The analysis utilizes a transient formulation incorporating the Backward-Euler discretization method. Contact interactions are modeled through a penalty approach combined with a Nitsche-type weak formulation to ensure natural implementation and improved stability, while nonlinearities are resolved via a Picard iteration scheme. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conc} provides a summary and offers an outlook on future research. This class is characterized by an invertible Beltrami flow combined with any steady state solution to the Poisson equation. These traveling waves move and translate uniformly across the entire plane, including scenarios where the wave profile shifts or moves. The analysis encompasses several significant subclasses, including: (i) all cat's-eye flows as traveling waves; (ii) a family of nontrivial smooth patch flows as traveling waves, where the speed can be calculated; and (iii) a family of compact helical flows as traveling waves, exhibiting either smooth or discontinuous profiles depending on specific parameters. This problem is then resolved using degree theory combined with a contradiction argument grounded in 2D elliptic theory. This approach identifies parameters where the large homogeneous Beltrami flow constitutes a degree-one perturbation of the Hilbert transform within any Sobolev space $H^s$ for $s>1$. The central challenge lies in proving this degree equals one. By expressing the Hilbert transform as the limit of operators with known degree and demonstrating its continuity with respect to the flow speed, we conclude that the degree remains unchanged. Health Organization (WHO) declared the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) a global pandemic, leading to widespread pandemic response measures (PRMs) across many countries to curb transmission. This study aims to quantify the impact of these measures, identify factors influencing their effectiveness, and propose an optimal strategy for maximum efficacy. By modeling the dynamic changes in COVID-19 cases alongside PRMs through a high-dimensional non-linear stochastic differential equation model, the research incorporates noise factors affecting public policies through the addition of stochastic terms. Estimation and optimization were conducted using real-world data from China, Russia, and South Korea. The study's novel contribution includes determining the most effective combination and implementation sequence of pandemic measures. Results indicate that the Chinese PRM strategy was highly effective, with the highest reduction in new cases attributed to face-to-face distance requirements (16.10%) and quarantine for foreign travelers (13.38%). In contrast, South Korean measures were less effective, with quarantine for travelers contributing the most to case reduction at 10.13%. The study concludes that Chinese public policies were significantly more effective than those of the other countries analyzed. Furthermore, the paper's theoretical advancement lies in the invariance of the COVID-19 model under general transformations involving time, infections, and PRMs, allowing for data estimation from transformed variables. Finally, the life expectancy of the disease was calculated for all three countries, determining that it averages 206 days. The full code is available for download at github.com/zeyadaal/COVID-19.

Question: What is the average life expectancy of the COVID-19 disease as calculated in this study? Answer: 206 days.

Question: Which country's pandemic response measure was found to be the most effective in reducing new cases? Answer: China.

Which country's public policy was determined to be the least effective in reducing new cases? Answer: South Korea.

The primary obstacle to training deep neural networks for natural language generation (NLG) is the scarcity of high-quality training data. Current data augmentation methods either demand extensive human labor to ensure relevance or suffer from the high statistical variability of standard text generation. We propose a solution that combines automated data generation with the filtering capabilities of pre-trained language models. Our results on the ISEAR and SETC datasets indicate that this strategy effectively merges the advantages of cost-effective and high-quality augmentation, yielding a 15% improvement in sentence-level creativity and significantly faster processing times compared to existing methods. is a common operation in embedded systems, including Digital Signal Processing. It can be optimized by substituting certain input values with left-shifted versions, defined as $2^k-1$, where the multiplier $x$ is replaced by $x \cdot 2^k$. This paper analyzes the fundamental trade-off between operational overhead and accuracy loss inherent in this approximation. A critical insight is that the relative error follows a bounded triangular distribution in both linear and multiple MCM contexts. Leveraging this finding, we introduce an exact and efficient sensitivity-based symbolic approach to calculate the worst-case relative error, avoiding the computational costs and inaccuracies associated with traditional inclusion-exclusion methods. This exact error calculation enables precise probability-based and risk-based decision-making. Furthermore, we derive closed-form formulas for the mean, variance, and bounded triangular distribution of errors for single and multiple MCM operations. These derived formulas facilitate an analytical evaluation of the benefits and constraints of MCM substitution, supporting both probabilistic and risk-driven design choices. The exact symbolic method is particularly valuable for the probabilistic approach, while the risk-based approach is ideal for multiple MCM scenarios. Numerical experiments validate the accuracy of our error calculation method and compare it against conventional techniques. Using these formulas, we also conduct a theoretical analysis of multiple MCM operations, determining optimal left-shift amounts and locating the maximum error point. Our conclusions indicate that the most significant error occurs at the $2/3^{\text{rd}}$ position relative to the normalized input range $[0,1]$, rather than at the boundaries or center. Consequently, test data for verifying MCM implementations should ideally be selected near this $2/3^{\text{rd}}$ point to ensure comprehensive coverage. Finally, we examine how to minimize the expected overall error in a multiple MCM implementation, revealing that the optimal substitution pattern for minimizing bounded relative error differs from that of minimizing mean relative error. Additionally, we investigate how to minimize the error with the highest probability, observing that the optimal strategy is a left-shift by 1 in nearly all cases. Numerical experiments confirm the efficacy of these proposed approaches. Furthermore, we evaluate the error reduction achievements across various scenarios for multiple MCM operations. In conclusion, our proposed methods offer a precise and efficient alternative to existing techniques for MCM optimization.

The most common radiofrequency waveforms used to drive the radiofrequency quadrupole (RFQ) are sine and square waves. However, because of their rich harmonic spectra, these traditional waveforms often demand precise phase relationships, necessitating complex feedback and synchronization systems to maintain correct timing for multibunch waveforms. This paper introduces a novel modulation technique known as asymmetric square wave (ASW) generation. This approach offers a low-cost, simple method for producing multibunch waveforms by utilizing a single digital-to-analog converter. The proposed method involves modulating a symmetric square wave with a sinusoidal envelope of varying amplitude to achieve the desired bunching. The study presents the design and experimental results of an ASW circuit, confirming its ability to replicate theoretical outcomes. Specifically, a 3-bunch ASW circuit was demonstrated with a final output amplitude of 2.5 V and an inter-bunch spacing error of less than 0.5%. Furthermore, the approach is scalable to generate any number of bunches—such as 5 or 7—by simply adjusting the relevant parameters. Finally, these waveforms are applicable to accelerator devices including the RFQ, radiofrequency septum, and chopper. This research was conducted at the Delhi Accelerator Technology Incubator (DATIN).

Key issues and challenges remain, but continued offtime R&D work could resolve most critical problems, paving the way for the design and construction phases during the next decade. the inaugural complete system dedicated to two-party Secure Division (SD). The SD problem involves two distrustful parties who must jointly determine a fair split of a value according to Nash demand game rules, where each party receives their minimum of what they demand and the solution (4/9, 2/9, 2/9, 2/9). While prior work has addressed computational and communication efficiency in specific models—such as honest execution, pre-established trust, Secure Function Evaluation (SFE), and Simultaneous Move (SIM)—no prior solution simultaneously achieves optimality across all four scenarios. Our results are as follows:

1. In honest execution, we present a fully synchronous protocol that is at least two orders of magnitude faster than the fastest pre-established trust model.
2. For pre-established trust, we demonstrate a significant improvement in communication complexity, achieving a reduction of more than 60%, thus surpassing the leading SFE model.
3. We provide a novel Simultaneous Move (SIM) protocol that is both simply understandable and highly efficient: it requires only 19 gates per party per round in the most complex round and transmits just 3 bits per party per round across all rounds.
4. We offer a comprehensive solution for Secure Division (SD) with optimal efficiency in every model. Notably, our SIM protocol is significantly faster than the best SFE approach (reducing computation by a factor exceeding 3). We further establish a new lower bound on communication complexity for Secure Division under SIM, showing that our protocol is within a factor of 2 of this bound while maintaining simplicity.

All our proposed solutions are either the simplest, the fastest, or the most efficient among the top-performing protocols in their respective categories. We confirm the platform's functionality through simulation and provide a deployment on a real testbed linking a physical server to a FPGA. This work not only advances theoretical understanding of Secure Division but also offers a new method for efficiently privatizing computations. By enabling individuals to safely divide valuable assets (like heirlooms) and reducing the cost of private data processing, these findings can benefit various fields, including economics and computer science. This paper shifts focus to address composite reasoning capabilities by utilizing planning tasks as a theoretical planning domain. To do this, we adapt the classic tile world planning problem for NLP by mapping it to language through *language planning*. We propose abstracting the specific features of the RAM that make it suitable for algorithmic definitions into a formal interface known as a Turing Interface (TI). This results in an operational semantics for algorithms that is both simpler and more intuitive than approaches to programming languages or abstract machines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any problem solvable in polynomial time on a RAM can also be solved in polynomial time on a specific TI consisting of a finite array of "cell computers," where each cell computer is essentially a two-state finite automaton. This finding offers a novel, intuitive characterization of P-time computability and contributes to resolving a question raised by M. Burgin and S. A. Kuznetsov in [3]. Although our result is effective, it does not provide explicit bounds on the time required by a RAM algorithm to simulate a TI algorithm. Consequently, it remains an open problem to determine the precise time bound on a TI that corresponds to a given polynomial $p$, a challenge crucial for adapting this characterization to competitive programming. The difficulty of this problem stems from the fact that a TI algorithm may require exponential time to evaluate a single step of a RAM algorithm. This phenomenon occurs because a TI algorithm operates in reverse: it guesses which operations a RAM algorithm performs and verifies them. This behavior can be understood as the source of co-NP-completeness in many problems solvable in polynomial time on the RAM, or as the mechanism enabling sublinear-time computation under the pseudo-polynomial time assumption. Finally, we examine the implications of these issues in the context of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. However, the specific computational function of recurrent information flow in these contexts remains poorly understood. This study examines RNNs trained for object categorization using microscopes to analyze how information propagates recursively. By employing network layers as black boxes and replacing them with linear, attention-free alternatives, we tested the necessity of recurrent connections, attention mechanisms, and nonlinearity. Our findings indicate that when attention is disabled, an RNN with roughly half the parameters of a feedforward network achieves comparable test set accuracy. Furthermore, attention becomes critical only in the final time step, where omitting it leads to a significant performance drop. These results suggest that attention is more essential for complex inputs, such as multi-object images, than for single objects. Additionally, we demonstrate that attention can be effectively approximated by dense linear transformations, implying that the heavy recurrent connectivity required by standard RNNs might stem from an unnecessary requirement to model intricate attention dynamics. Consequently, this research offers a new perspective on designing computationally efficient and biologically plausible models for object categorization. By highlighting the reduced need for recurrent information flow when attention is absent, our work offers an alternative to the prevalent assumption that attention is the primary driver of recurrent effects in the visual system during object recognition.

We introduce a topological framework centered on the winding of off-diagonal density winding numbers (odwns) within a one-dimensional chain of interacting fermions. Through numerical analysis, we determined that while many-body fermionic correlations in the non-interacting topological phase break inversion symmetry and alter the winding number pattern—resulting in four distinct integers instead of two—these patterns can still resolve the phase transition. Furthermore, we established a rigorous framework for calculating odwns in interacting systems and successfully applied it to determine the winding number in a chain of interacting Rashba-wired fermions. Finally, we numerically investigated the competition between inversion symmetry breaking and the acquisition of odd winding numbers in these interacting systems. Our findings indicate that the inversion symmetry-breaking effect on odwns is secondary, allowing the system to reach its ground state by sequentially acquiring both even and odd winding numbers. This outcome aligns with the non-interacting analysis, where the topological phase is governed by sign changes in the odd winding numbers and the inversion symmetric ground state is achieved. These results demonstrate that the competition between breaking effects and ground state acquisition is effectively managed by 1D non-Hermitian topology, providing a new perspective on the topological ordering in one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems with interactions.

In this scenario, the new heavy Higgs doublet is assumed to be heavy, enabling the effective low-energy description of its integrated-out effects. We analyze various production production modes and associated signals at the HL-LHC and ATP. Our results indicate that relative to the SM and Simple Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (S2HDM), both signal rates increase by up to approximately two orders of magnitude in certain parameter regions. Specifically, low values of the additional Higgs doublet mass ($m_X$) and large $m_X$-Higgs coupling constants drive these signals to the largest deviations from the SM. These findings suggest that both models could be discovered within the first LHC run by early data releases at the HL-LHC and ATP. Furthermore, excluding parameters in regions where new physics couplings are as large or larger than the SM, the two models are highly testable. Consequently, these hypotheses are significantly more predictive than the generic assumption of universally large couplings. We also note that the C2HDM and S2HDM are potentially disambiguated through measurements of Higgs self couplings and electroweak precision observables. Finally, despite potential signal enhancements, both models face significant background challenges in heavy Higgs searches, with the signal cross sections in those categories remaining in the femtobarn range or lower. These points are explicitly addressed in our discussion of heavy Higgs searches. Any model in quantum field theory can be reformulated classically by replacing fields with collections of particles. For instance, a scalar field becomes a system of scalar particles, while a spinor field yields spinor particles. Consequently, particles derived from free quantum Hall edge modes, which carry statistical phases, appear to contradict the standard arguments regarding the existence of particles in a classical field. In this work, we clarify this issue by examining a model of moving particles in two dimensions with a half-integer flux tube. We find that while these particles possess non-trivial statistical phases when well-separated, they exhibit trivial statistics at large distances. This loss of phase memory can be interpreted in two ways: either as a direct absence of particles carrying well-defined statistics, or as the emergence of new particles with trivial statistics that annihilate the phases originally held by the original particles. \section{Introduction}

Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) serve as the foundational framework for sequential decision-making. Within an MDP, an agent interacts with an environment by selecting actions to maximize cumulative rewards. However, in many real-world scenarios, the transition dynamics are unknown, and exploring the entire state-action space is impractical. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a solution by enabling agents to learn policies directly from data; nonetheless, raw RL methods often demand excessive sample sizes.

To address this, Model-Based RL (MBRL) employs a transition model to predict environmental dynamics and compute an optimal policy. By simulating future trajectories in the local model, MBRL can derive a policy that generalizes to the true environment, often achieving higher sample efficiency than model-free techniques. Various techniques have been developed to estimate transition models, including Kullback-based regression \cite{zou2019model}, variational approaches \cite{tamar2017less}, and graph neural networks \cite{shie2019learning}. Although these methods successfully generate a local model that approximates the true dynamics, they generally fail to account for measurement noise.

In contrast to model \emph{parametric} learning \cite{zou2019model}, Bayesian Learning (BL) aims to infer a probability distribution over parameters \cite{tamar2017less}. Similarly, Bayesian Regression (BR) focuses on predicting a distribution for targets. ### I. INTRODUCTION

Collision avoidance is critical for the successful deployment of the Internet of Things (IoT) and is therefore a fundamental requirement of multi-robot navigation. Numerous solutions have been proposed, ranging from heuristic methods to model-predictive control. Given the rise of autonomous delivery systems like those used by Amazon, it is essential that vehicle trajectories be computable and safe given the robot's dynamics and the anticipated motion of obstacles. Moreover, the method must remain robust against drifts and errors in obstacle state estimates to maintain safety guarantees. Most notably, existing methods often fail to account for the multi-dimensional space of mobile robots.

Given these considerations, we address the following problem:

> We develop a model-predictive control law, utilizing the robot's full spatial dimensions, to guarantee safe navigation of mobile robots within a multi-robot environment containing static obstacles.

Safety is defined such that no obstacle-collision occurs during navigation. As demonstrated in the proof, this guarantee holds for every dimension of the robot's configuration space, encompassing both orientation (e.g., orientation-obstacle collision) and projection on the ground (e.g., corner collision). To the best of our knowledge, existing literature does not guarantee safety for all configuration variables.

Given the limitations of current approaches, we pose two questions:
> 1) Do existing methods guarantee safety for all robot configuration variables?
> 2) If not, can we guarantee safety for all configuration variables?

This study investigates the acceleration of electrons within pulsar wind zones (PWZs) using P-wave one-magneton solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation. We find that these solutions facilitate electron acceleration to high energies when electrons are confined to magnetic field lines situated at large distances from pulsars. This work presents the spectrum of a z=10.6 AGN discovered within the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array "Tiny Tim Test of Near Infrared Spectroscopy" (ATTICS) ultra-deep field. We conducted a spectroscopic analysis of the object using its newly acquired JWST Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) high-resolution data. We successfully identified low-ionization emission lines in the spectrum, with [O III] 5287 Angstrom separating from the continuum at a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 5. Furthermore, we measured equivalent widths for [O III] and [Ne V] exceeding 30 A, values characteristic of star-forming regions and high-ionization non-star-forming sources. Additionally, we determined a stellar mass of log(M*/M_sun) = 5.0 (+3/-2), indicating that the galaxy hosting this record-breaking AGN was already significantly massive at z>10.6. This finding supports prior suggestions of log(M*/M_sun)>4 as a minimum mass threshold for high-z AGN host galaxies. Our results confirm the existence of extremely massive and highly luminous young galaxies in the earliest universe, highlighting low-ionization AGNs as a previously unidentified class of distant extragalactic objects. The AGN detected in ATTICS-02 represents either the most distant low-ionization AGN known to date, or the second such object if the source of ATTICS-01 is indeed extragalactic. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent's own historical successful trajectories alongside a small number of external demonstrations. These demonstrations can originate from various sources, such as expert-generated paths, the agent's past sub-optimal attempts, or data generated by imitation models. The primary objective of CoIL is to discover a strategy that maximizes the frequency of visiting high-reward states during execution, rather than strictly matching full trajectories. The core innovative contribution is a Coily clustering algorithm that generates a subset of strategy networks for each CoIL instance. This algorithm determines the most beneficial strategies to visit high-reward states by analyzing both external demonstrations and intrinsic agent experiences. Extensive experiments conducted in a continuous MuJoco walking environment demonstrate that CoIL significantly outperforms baseline methods, including standard imitation learning, when trained with sub-optimal histories combined with external demonstrations. These results highlight CoIL's potential for practical applications where obtaining optimal trajectories from all available agents is impossible. Furthermore, we provide a straightforward proof-of-coneup code for the CoIL framework, which delivers competitive performance compared to existing similar projects.

### I. INTRODUCTION

Convolutional codes remain one of the earliest and most extensively utilized forward error correction techniques, with their performance historically governed by the signal-to-noise ratio. The Viterbi algorithm, the primary decoding method, operates as a maximum-likelihood technique with a complexity of $O(N_LN)$, where $N$ represents the total states and $L$ the memory length. While numerous studies have addressed complexity reduction—particularly through the truncation of the search process—few have focused on enhancing the underlying metric function to achieve superior performance. This study addresses two vital areas: first, developing an optimized average metric function for convolutional codes via truncated Viterbi decoding, and second, extending this framework to code combinations using a similar methodology. Our objectives are threefold: to enhance the overall metric function, shorten decoding delay, and, in the case of truncated Viterbi decoding, further lower complexity. The proposed scheme was tested on a 7-rate convolutional code with generator polynomials $(227, 133, 171, 133, 151, 171, 133, 151)$ and an 8-rate code with polynomials $(223, 181, 181, 181, 181, 181, 181, 181)$. Results indicate a substantial reduction in both complexity and decoding delay. The authors also propose a similar analysis for LDPC codes, with outcomes detailed in our joint work [1].

In particular, we present a simpler and more intuitive algorithm achieving $m \operatorname{polylog} n$ time, and we identify additional opportunities to accelerate other approximate algorithms by clarifying the role of space complexity. Moreover, our results indicate that the current best-known lower bound of $\Omega(f(\epsilon)m \operatorname{polylog} n)$ for $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate single-source shortest paths in unweighted undirected graphs is likely tight. In model predictive control, ensuring constraint satisfaction for nonlinear dynamical systems with potential safety risks is vital. Recently, safety filters have emerged as a promising solution to enforce constraints on potentially unsafe control signals. Since safety filters depend on the system's dynamics, deriving their values can be computationally demanding for complex models. To address this, we utilize raul and Olfati-Saber's state-space formulation and model reduction approach to compute safety filters with improved efficiency. Our method is demonstrated using raul and Olfati-Saber's form of the safety filter defined by Olfati-Saber and Teo's work, applied to a second-order system with constraints on the control input and its derivative. The study compares the computational complexity and performance of the original versus reduced state-space representations. Furthermore, we integrate this technique with raul and Olfati-Saber's ratcheting algorithm to enforce constraints on the time-derivative of the control input, a use case previously unexplored by the authors. This ratcheting implementation has also been applied to a inverted pendulum model. We show that our method reduces the computation time required for safety filter calculation by over 90%. This achievement is realized by solving an optimisation problem with fewer variables, which involves evaluating the system's future states and derivatives based on the proposed state-space representation. We verify the effectiveness and computational efficiency of our method through implementation on both linear and nonlinear dynamical systems.

This paper presents a novel motion control framework for aerial vehicles navigating narrow gaps defined by static obstacles. The controller comprises two distinct feedback laws: a local gap-tracking law and a global guidance law, integrated via a switching mechanism. The local law ensures accurate tracking of a reference trajectory around the gap using only output feedback and a finite-time robustness property derived from the reaching phase of a non-singular terminal sliding mode controller. The switching surface is modified to enforce robustness against disturbances during the transition between control laws, while the global law guarantees asymptotic convergence to a desired orbit around the gap. Extensive numerical simulations and experimental tests were conducted to validate the proposed scheme's robustness, accuracy, and real-time performance. Additionally, an open-source implementation of the controller is provided.

A key challenge in aerial vehicle navigation and aerial photography is the accurate estimation of the relative position and orientation of a target of interest (TO). This paper proposes a new relative state estimator designed for aerial vehicles navigating around targets to capture high-quality images from multiple viewpoints. A extended Kalman filter (EKF) estimates the range and line-of-sight (LOS) angle to the TO, while a sliding mode observer compensates for unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances affecting the estimation error. The overall estimator is proven to be robust, and an integral form of the sliding surface enhances the robustness of the sliding mode observer. The proposed scheme's efficacy is verified via numerical simulations and experimental tests on a real quadrotor platform. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of the estimator.

We demonstrate that for any convex and $ \gamma $-smooth function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, there exists a regularized distributionally robust learning task featuring a $ \gamma $-convex objective function. Specifically, the task involves a symmetric family of probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a regularized loss function defined as the pointwise maximum of $f$ and the label, i.e., $\max \{ f(x), y \}$. It is sufficient for the input distributions of the true probability measure to be symmetric. By formulating the learning problem as a minimax objective, we establish that:
a) the optimal value is equivalent to the optimal value of a regularized learning task using an asymmetric $f$ and the non-regularized loss function $f$;
b) the optimal solution corresponds to the solution of the original regularized learning task.
Furthermore, since many asymmetric functions can be transformed into symmetric ones via appropriate coordinate choices, these findings enable the reduction of numerous regularized distributionally robust learning problems to a single type. Additionally, the results provide theoretical support for the effectiveness of bootstrap techniques in this context.
In summary, our contributions are:
- A theoretical framework unifying multiple methods for regularized distributionally robust learning.
- An explanation of the connection between the bootstrap method in learning theory and the distributionally robust learning task.
- Insights into the link between the regularized dual of a convex optimization problem and a "bigger" problem involving the original (non-regularized) objective function.
These points are illustrated for the single-sample case, thereby integrating bootstrap theory, regularized distributionally robust learning, and optimal transport.
Finally, we establish that the optimal input distribution for the true measure must be unimodal and propose an algorithm to identify the unique solution.

In strongly magnetized clouds, powerful, high-velocity jets (excessively >200 km s$^{-1}$) are produced even with low mass accretion rates, suggesting that strongly self-gravitating molecular cores typically eject high-speed jets during star formation. Conversely, weak magnetic fields or high mass accretion rates limit the mass ratio $\dot{M}_{\rm jet}/\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$ during protostar formation while still enabling the direct collapse of gas onto the protostar without requiring jets. The momentum coupling ratio $p_{\rm jet}/\dot{E}_{\rm jet}$ for high-speed jets reaches approximately 0.2, aligning closely with observational estimates for observed protostellar jets. Derived sound speeds within jets from self-gravitating cores with weak magnetic fields are significantly lower than in strongly magnetized cores with low mass accretion rates, potentially explaining the diversity seen in observed jets. These findings indicate that self-gravitating molecular cores with weak magnetic fields often produce slow jets that fail to regulate star formation efficiency during the protostar formation phase.

The proposed strategy involves optimizing the total capacity of the category, defined as the sum of the system's equilibrium output when all agents operate at their limits relative to the sum of individual agent capacities. In recent years, vector auto-regressions (VARs) have been widely used in macroeconomics for model identification and forecasting, with interest intensifying as researchers seek to incorporate state space representations into DSGE frameworks that remain unobservable to central banks. However, the primary limitation of VAR models is their inability to account for structural breaks, a task for which the Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) technique is a logical choice. The main obstacles to applying BMA to VAR models are the computational intensity of estimating a large number of candidate models and the complexity involved in switching between them. This study presents a solution by reformulating the BMA procedure as a state space problem and employing a specialized MCMC algorithm that can remain stuck in a specific model for an extended period without incurring excessive computation time. Our findings indicate that this BMA model outperforms the standard optimal-order VAR in both in-sample estimation and out-of-sample forecasting. Additionally, we find that BMA effectively identifies a specific set of persistent variables that best represent the business cycle.

A critical step toward this goal involves determining the potential instability scale of the Higgs field. This requires significantly reducing uncertainties regarding the strong coupling constant and the top quark mass. We demonstrate that the top quark mass can be measured with sufficient precision through a $t \bar t$ threshold scan, achievable with a luminosity of approximately $10^{33}\,{\rm cm}^{-2}{\rm sec}^{-1}$. We conclude by comparing these proposals against other existing or proposed experimental initiatives. Ultimately, such a collider would serve as an essential complement to the LHC and serve as a precursor for a muon collider.

Current approaches typically rely on extracting features from overlapping patches or utilizing over-segmentation algorithms to divide images into parts, after which instance features are extracted and clustered to identify distinct instances. However, because these methods often fail to capture long-range dependencies and boundary information, they result in inaccurate segmentations and incorrect annotations of individual instances. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel weakly supervised instance segmentation algorithm designed for domain transfer, termed Boundary-Aware Graph Attention Network (BAGAN). This model is driven by spatially aligned patch overlap graphs (PGs) and boundary-Aware graphs (BGs), where boundary information is isolated through edge detection graphs (EDGs). BGs and EDGs are integrated into PGs to enable boundary-aware feature learning, accurate feature representation, and precise feature clustering for instance segmentation. Experimental results on public datasets (XrayCT and USR) for domain transfer demonstrate that boundary awareness significantly improves segmentation accuracy and the correctness of instance annotations, with BAGAN achieving an average improvement of approximately 10%. These performance gains make BAGan highly promising for practical, cost-effective application in biomedical image analysis.

The behavior of these compositum systems is significantly influenced by the axiomatization of identity. Although Leibniz have historically treated identity as a non-logical axiom to facilitate the interpretation of linear orders, this approach creates obstacles for arithmetic applications. To address this, we propose treating identity as a logical axiom; specifically, this involves adding an expression for reflexivity to the basic logic and defining the identity relation to satisfy the standard properties of reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. Our findings indicate that while identity remains equivalent to the statements "everything is identical to itself" and "distinct elements are unique" in most logics, this equivalence does not hold in others. Furthermore, when combined with a order similarity axiom, the resulting logical order properties—such as density and minimality—are preserved across interpretations between distinct logics. Finally, the interaction between identity and non-logical axioms has crucial implications for the interpretability of Peano Arithmetic and other arithmetic systems. Specifically, the choice of how identity is axiomatized determines which foundational systems can be interpreted within others like Peano Arithmetic. Notably, interpretations involving many-sorted logics, such as that of, present challenges for proving the interpretability of Peano Arithmetic. However, by utilizing standard (monosorted) logics, we can interpret Peano Arithmetic in similar systems without increasing either the language or the number of sorts.

named Split Parallel (SP), designed to accelerate the training of deep neural networks (DNNs) by effectively linking small-scale distributed training and federated learning. To ensure privacy by preventing raw training data from leaving users' devices, SP incorporates a specialized local training algorithm that utilizes mini-batches of non-identically distributed (NID) data. By extracting the underlying connection between these NID mini-batches and standard identically distributed (IID) data, the model is trained using aggregated outputs from both users and the center without accessing any individual user's raw data. Additionally, we developed an efficient quantization algorithm to reduce communication overhead required by the updated sparse models. Experimental results on various real-world datasets demonstrate that SP outperforms comparable federated learning methods by up to 2.66 times and exceeds single-GPU training speeds by up to 1.61 times. To validate SP's practical applicability, we applied it to two prominent computer vision tasks: object classification and semantic segmentation. The source code will be made publicly available. SP is highly versatile and can be easily adapted for various other visual intelligence applications, making it ideal for large-scale, real-world scenarios where the volume of training data is distributed across users' local devices.

This study examines a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system where Wada basin boundaries transition to non-Wada configurations once the critical energy threshold is exceeded, assuming no dissipation. Specifically, we investigate how dissipation influences this topological shift, a phenomenon with no equivalent in two dimensions. Our findings reveal that non-Wada basins, anticipated in the dissipationless regime, evolve into partially Wada basins when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below the critical level. Numerical evidence supports the emergence of Wada points on basin boundaries under these conditions. We conclude that in three-dimensional open Hamiltonian systems, Wada basins are typically driven, enhanced, and structurally stabilized by weak dissipation. This represents a fundamental difference from general two-dimensional scenarios, leading us to propose that the "dissipative paradox" observed in two dimensions may also operate in three dimensions. Finally, these insights are expected to be applicable within various other three-dimensional chaotic scattering models. Additionally, we present a theoretical framework for the rare occurrence of truly non-Wada basins in three-dimensional systems with weak dissipation. While experimentally verifying Wada points or cells remains challenging in three dimensions compared to two, we argue that the insights derived here could facilitate such verifications in both experimental and computational settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the complex dissipation-induced evolution of Wada basets is also present in the general relativistic three-body problem. This research holds potential value for fields including general physics, mathematical physics, and astrophysical physics. Additionally, our work could inspire analogous investigations across other complex physical systems, both with and without dissipation, and even within quantum physics and quantum computing, as appropriate. As the sophistication of attack methods, the diversity of attackers, and the vastness of the cyber domain expand, the demand for novel and efficient countermeasures has also grown. However, most current CSD approaches are reactive, relying on the detection of specific attack signatures or patterns. Extensive simulations were conducted using the ISA-100.011 standard critical infrastructure testbed to evaluate APOLLO's performance. The results demonstrate that APOLLO achieves swift system recovery after an attack, increases the time required for attackers to compromise critical systems, and enhances overall system resilience. to build predictive models that guide therapeutic decisions. A primary category of these models, known as prognostic models, estimates the future course of a disease. Teratoma formation represents a significant complication in Intrauterine Pneumothorax (IUP), yet no predictive model currently exists to assist clinicians. This study introduces a prognostic model designed to assist clinicians in determining whether an infant developing IUP requires invasive therapeutic interventions. The model was constructed using data from 29 infants (both left and right lungs) gathered between 2006 and 2 Unilateral Intrauterine Pneumothorax. During the observation period, 11 infants (38%) developed chorioamnionitis, a condition defined by one or more additional risk factors beyond uterine compression. At birth, infants with chorioamnionitis exhibited significantly higher rates of teratoma (45% vs. 18%, p < 0.05), larger lung compression (4.06 ± 0.86 mmHg vs. 3.27 ± 0.86 mmHg, p < 0.05), and higher occurrence of preterm birth (<37 weeks) (64% vs. 29%, p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis, adjusted for laterality and gestational age, confirmed that chorioamnionitis is an independent predictor for teratoma, with high sensitivity (91%) and specificity (82%). A point-system model was designed to categorize infants into three risk levels for teratoma: Low Risk (all points <3), Moderate Risk (at least one point =3), and High Risk (at least one point >3). The model demonstrates two distinct outcomes: 86% of infants (65 out of 76) remained teratoma-free after 2 weeks, while 14% (11 out of 76) developed teratoma. Furthermore, the model is highly discriminative, achieving a C-index of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.69–0.96). In conclusion, this point-system model effectively predicts teratoma development in infants with IUP, enabling the timely initiation of appropriate therapies.

This experimental data serves as a foundation for the \textit{expressive kernel principal component analysis (KPCA)} algorithm, which successfully reconstructs eigenvectors up to mid-frequencies. However, the algorithm's computational complexity scales quadratically with the number of measured frequency components, rendering it impractical for high-frequency applications. To address this, we adapt the traditional \textit{deflation kernel principal component analysis (DKPCA)} method, modified to prioritize accuracy over speed, for the reconstruction of high-frequency eigenvectors from glassy silicon. Comparisons with \textit{discrete polar decomposition (DPD)} and the original KPCA algorithm show that this modified DKPCA is both faster and more accurate than the latter two. Although slightly less precise than KPCA for lower frequencies, the modified DKPCA algorithm remains computationally feasible, making it an essential tool for analyzing gigahertz vibrations in amorphous materials. Furthermore, this approach is broadly applicable to any technique capable of experimentally determining the spectra of localized modes and their associated mode shapes. By combining the newly reported modified DKPCA method with the original DKPCA variant for speed, we demonstrate its effectiveness in reliably and efficiently recovering full vibrational modes up to the glass transition frequency. Relatively small, mode-incomplete datasets yield reliable reconstructions, with the mode envelope typically within \sim1\% of the simulated values at the maximum measured frequency. This represents a significant advancement over the state-of-the-art DKPCA method, which is approximately ten times slower and exhibits roughly \sim10\% root mean square error at the same frequency threshold. This represents a crucial capability for the general analysis of experimental data regarding glassy materials. Furthermore, we show that DKPCA can robustly and accurately recover complete modes even from random, incomplete data. This capability offers a new tool for the field of inverse design in materials science, with broad implications for various spectroscopic techniques including inelastic x-ray scattering and electron energy-loss spectroscopy. Ultimately, these algorithms will greatly facilitate the global analysis of experimental datasets and deepen our understanding of the structures and dynamics within amorphous materials. Consequently, developing rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling faulty syndrome measurements is essential. This study demonstrates that decoding these codes within a full fault-tolerant framework can be naturally recast as repeated interactions between a decoder and its environment, enabling the application of reinforcement learning to train decoding agents. As a proof of concept, we utilized deep Q-learning to create fast decoding agents for the surface code across various noise models. We established that deep Q-learning can effectively manage frameworks involving faulty syndrome measurements and presented several accelerated decoding strategies. Our results show that deep Q-learning achieves fault-tolerance thresholds comparable to those of sophisticated analytical codes like the minimum weight perfect matching algorithm. Furthermore, we developed a RNN-based minimum weight perfect matching decoder that operates approximately 100 times faster while maintaining similar performance. These findings indicate that reinforcement learning holds significant promise as a general-purpose method for producing both rapid and adaptive decoding solutions.

In this scheme, digital segments are combined with analog evolution units, where the latter conditionally evolve qubit states based on the parity of qubit pairs. This parity-dependent evolution, governed by an analog parameter, approximates Hadamard gates and CNOT operations with high precision. By stochastically shuffling circuit layers and leveraging the continuity of analog evolution, we demonstrate that unitary gates can be approximately decomposed. Since analog integration and digital segments are implemented through distinct physical mechanisms, randomized measurements and error correction can effectively detect and correct computational errors. We establish that any quantum computation can be approximated to any desired accuracy and conclude that this hybrid approach is viable whenever a continuous family of qubit interactions can be isolated and controlled independently from other interactions. This paves the way for implementing quantum computations on various emerging hardware platforms. As a specific proof of concept, we show that the scheme can be realized on trapped ions by applying microwaves to individual ions while inducing conditional dynamics via their spatially varying motional mode. The trained control parameters are detailed in Supplementary Information. For universal computation, the method requires $O(\log^{2} (1/\epsilon))$ microseconds of ion interaction time, with an error rate approximately $100$ times lower than the errors typically encountered in variational quantum algorithms on this platform. Furthermore, the digital-analog protocol can accelerate the T-gate synthesis necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computation, a capability that is also critical for smoothing the transition from experimental prototypes to fault-tolerant machines. The approach offers several advantages over purely digital universal quantum computing and is applicable to a broad spectrum of alternative hardware, including other trapped ion configurations, other atomic systems, and superconducting circuits. By approximating these gates through analog integration, we enable faster and more efficient implementation of quantum algorithms and error correction protocols. robust generalization for out-of-distribution (OoD) detection in deep neural networks. Addressing this, we observe that effective OoD detection requires moving beyond minimizing pure observation loss, which tends to overfit. Instead, we propose minimizing the generalization risk of OoD observations, defined as the difference in classification accuracy between OoD and in-distribution samples, to enhance the classifier's robustness against OoD inputs. However, minimizing this generalization risk is not straightforward, as the true OoD data distribution is typically unknown, and it is impossible to directly compute the accuracy gap on data that is guaranteed to be out-of-distribution. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a self-generated OoD data generation process, which is theoretically proven to converge to a stationary distribution that is sufficiently far from the in-distribution data. Under this framework, we also derive a generation complexity analysis, offering a novel perspective on the trade-off between the ease of optimization and the robustness of the resulting classifier against OoD inputs. Extensive experiments across various architectures and datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, demonstrate that our method effectively identifies OoD observations and significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/dusongzhang/OOD-generation}.

We also examine the dynamic fluctuations in the velocity of a water jet passing through a coaxial honey syrup stream within a confined channel. Since our jets are electrically conductive, we tracked their trajectory using an external current circuit. Our results show that both penitration time and velocity fluctuations intensify as the relative viscosity of the jet increases. Conversely, neither penitration time nor velocity fluctuations are affected by changes in the jet's density or diameter. However, the intensity of these fluctuations scales positively with the relative penitration time and the relative viscosity, while remaining independent of the relative channel width.

We selected a setup involving a water jet (active) moving through a honey syrup stream (passive), assuming the honey's much higher viscosity prevents it from becoming entrained in the water stream. We observed that both regimes are independent of the jet's density but dependent on its initial velocity and diameter.
