The growing prevalence of Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) within these systems creates a challenge: NVM features a limited capacity for preserving critical data necessary for runtime recovery, a property that is inherently unreliable. This paper introduces a method integrated into the MPI library that leverages MPI intermediate buffers and NVM's persistent capabilities to establish a low-overhead, multi-rank fault tolerance mechanism dependent solely on collective operations. We implemented this approach using CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) policy-based design within CRPE (Composite Reusable Pattern), an extensible middleware framework developed at UBLM. Our implementation, referred to as MBNVM, was evaluated via a prototype built with CRPE and tested using OpenMPI on two platforms: a small desktop system equipped with Intel Xeon W-2145 NVM servers and ScaleMP MP1 systems, with results discussed in this paper. OpenMPI was also tested against MBNVM, and the findings indicate that MBNVM offers superior performance and reliability compared to the standard OpenMPI solution. Additionally, a basic benchmark was conducted to examine the impact of the number of checks performed during NVM persistence. This test reveals a slight increase in fault tolerance overhead relative to the count of collective operations. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that MBNVM can identify and manage multiple concurrent failures. The official code for MBNVM and its accompanying test suite, including the test data files, are accessible at: https://github.com/UUBLM/MBNVM.

By applying an organizational ontology that defines entities based on structures, processes, and the control of those processes, we conclude that viruses are indeed organisms. We address these issues by distinguishing between individual organisms and the kind an organism belongs to. Our analysis suggests that ribozymes are not organisms, while plasmodia are eukaryotes. The apparent contradictions among these conclusions stem from the fact that organizational ontology relies on inter-level essentialism when describing biological kinds. To resolve this tension between using inter-level essentialism for kinds and individual-level location-based precision for organisms, we propose a solution that clearly defines the type of essentialism required. Individual organisms do not possess essentialist kinds, but their kinds do possess essentialist types. Since no true contradiction exists, this approach successfully resolves the contradictions identified. Finally, we note that the specific type of essentialism discussed is functional, a concept that can be re-introduced into the metaphysics of kinds to characterize both individual and kind-level entities.

This achievement addresses the primary unresolved question left by Bacci et al. (2018). These results may inspire future research on infinite programs or other probabilistic models. Finally, the paper examines the extension to other stochastic lambda calculi found in the literature.

The remainder of this section outlines the framework for higher-order probabilistic programs based on the extension to stochastic relations described in \cite{hansku2018}, with a primary focus on expectation instead of realization. As demonstrated in \cite{hansku2018}, this perspective offers a robust foundation for interpreting expressive probabilistic programs by ensuring the existence of sufficient measurements to detect any non-trivial effect of higher-order functions on expected values. However, the authors also highlight a significant limitation of this approach: it abstracts away from individual realizations, making it difficult to determine what occurs at the level of specific outcomes.

To investigate this issue, \cite{hansku2017} proposed a stochastic lambda calculus where higher-order terms represent transitions of a Markov chain defined by their action on path expectations, while first-order terms correspond to measurable functions. The authors argued that extending the language to incorporate higher-order measurable functions would be inappropriate, as such functions are generally not computable and thus incompatible with the operational semantics focused on specific executions. Nevertheless, many subsequent applications of the stochastic lambda calculus rely on higher-order functions to interpret program expressions, necessitating such an extension.

60% of all commits modify files that remain unchanged for a decade or more, a phenomenon known as "code archaeology." This longevity is frequently attributed to the software development lifecycle, where design decisions in old code often outlive the software itself. However, other explanations exist. In this paper, we present evidence that file age is a stronger predictor of post-merger activity than the issues addressed by a pull request (PR). We examine two scenarios for this correlation: first, that archaeologists ignore modern design features, and second, that they intentionally avoid them. For both cases, we develop and compare predictive models to test these hypotheses. Our findings indicate that the archaeologist effect is indeed valid, but file age still significantly influences commit frequency even after accounting for it. Our code and data are available at http://www.cs.brown.edu/~ant1/CodeArcheologyMining/.

Notably, when a monotone variational inequality (MVI) problem can be reformulated as a monotone variational inequality with merit function, a proximal point method may be applied. This study introduces a proximal interior point (PIP) algorithm designed for solving MVI problems within a closed, convex set. The algorithm generates Feasible Exterior Feasible (FEF) iterates, meaning the iterations may temporarily lie outside the feasible set. Under the standard assumption of the existence of at least one feasible point, we prove global convergence to a solution for PIP applied to Lipschitz continuous acid problems with bounded feasible sets. Bounded feasibility is verified through the upper boundedness of the algorithm's merit function values. By extending the use of the Lyapunov function, we establish convergence rates of $O(1/k)$ and $O(1/k \log k)$ for Lipschitz continuous and strongly Lipschitz continuous problems, respectively. Several well-known interior point algorithms are essentially special cases of the PIP algorithm. Furthermore, we recast numerous classical MVI problems—包括 Variance-Reduced Gradient Descent (VRGD), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Extragradient Algorithm (EGA)—as MVI problems to utilize the proposed PIP approach. Numerical experiments confirm that our PIP algorithm is competitive against traditional interior and feasible exterior methods. Finally, we highlight that our results for PIP are distinct from recent work by Li, Schönböck, and Tseng, as we resolve two open problems they identified while providing a unified framework for MVI problems. Specifically, our approach solves an MVI problem using a proximal algorithm while ensuring all iterations are feasible, and it achieves a convergence rate of $O(1/k)$, which is an improvement over the $O(1/\sqrt{k})$ rate reported in their work. *Key words*: Monotone variational inequality, Proximal algorithm, Feasible exterior point, Convergence rate. *10.2020 Mathematics Subject Classification*: 90C33, 90C25, 49J55.

\begin{abstract}
We present a unique technique for probing vacuum fluctuations compressed via photonic crystal fibers (PCF). This methodology relies on the fiber's dispersion characteristics around its zero-index frequency. Our results indicate that a minimal fiber length of a few millimeters is required to detect nonclassical properties in two-mode compressed vacuum. This approach holds promise for detecting vacuum compression at frequencies where nonclassical effects are otherwise inaccessible. Furthermore, the method is applicable to other systems exhibiting nonclassical behavior, such as two-mode nonlinear processes, quantum correlations, and entanglement.
\end{abstract}

We demonstrate that the former hypothesis predicts the existence of a universal slope for the stellar mass distribution, whereas the latter does not. This result suggests that an active regulation mechanism is operating during star formation, even if it is not the primary driver of the discrepancy between the two mass distributions. We demonstrate that when $\kash$ is sufficiently small, exhaustive enumeration can be performed in linear time relative to the total number of discoverable association rules. We establish upper and lower bounds for this parameter and develop a algorithm to calculate it. The smallness of $\kash$ corresponds to low two-dimensional density in the database. We illustrate the applicability of our findings across various database types, including arithmetic, bivariate, and random instances. Ultimately, our results enable the efficient enumeration of association rules for small-dimensional databases. While extending this theory to larger dimensions remains computationally infeasible, our work supports the development of heuristic methods for approximate rule enumeration and allows for the rapid computation of associations in databases with a limited number of transactions. Furthermore, our findings have implications for data storage and preprocessing, such as rapidly identifying all associations in a new database added to an existing collection. Any enumeration algorithm capable of utilizing this parameter can also be adapted to enumerate all perfect matchings in a bipartite graph where one partition has a limited cardinality. Additionally, our framework applies to the enumeration of transactions (or closed items) that satisfy specific properties, such as having asymmetric supports. This capability is essential for detecting database anomalies. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this method in a data quality control procedure.

visually analyzing the temporal dynamics of complex systems. This study presents the first, to our knowledge, ranked-correlation analysis of the temporal behaviors captured in radio astronomy. Our findings indicate that the coherence between the temporal behaviors of different galaxies varies on the gigahertz scale. Specifically, at low frequencies (a few hundred MHz), there is marginally significant correlation among all galaxies, whereas at higher frequencies (a few GHz), no significant correlation persists. This marginal significance at the lowest frequencies aligns with expectations, as radio emissions in the decimeter range are believed to originate from cosmic rays accelerated by sources such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. In contrast, our results offer evidence supporting the hypothesis of in-situ acceleration of GZK protons, which subsequently pair-produce gamma rays through photon-photon interactions with the cosmic microwave background. Furthermore, our results constrain the size of putative accretion disks surrounding supermassive black holes to be smaller than a light year. Finally, our work demonstrates the potential utility of radio astronomy data in uncovering the formation mechanisms of cosmic rays and gamma rays within high-energy astrophysics. Additionally, our work validates the feasibility of applying ranked correlation methods to assess synchronicity in complex systems.

Base classifiers are fundamental to many transfer-learning and multi-task learning systems. Although base classifier selection is a well-studied area, previous research has largely focused on optimizing for accuracy within a single predefined task. In our proposed adaptive selection approach, a base classifier's role and the task it handles emerge from the data rather than being defined in advance. We show that using such a selected classifier is equivalent to training one from scratch but with an attention mechanism focused on data regions the classifier deems important. Experiments confirm that our method selects a classifier that improves performance across multiple tasks compared to standard approaches. Additionally, we demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in removing artifacts from images and sequential data by focusing on salient content. Cross-entropy loss is a standard loss function for neural network-based machine learning. Its success stems from its strong theoretical connection to probability theory. However, in deep learning, cross-entropy is frequently combined with other loss functions and optimized using approximate techniques like stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches. This study examines cross-entropy in the context of a neural network's final layer, proving that under specific, recently introduced conditions, minimizing cross-entropy is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the posterior probability of a sample given the network. These conditions suggest that certain neural network components, like dense layers, should ideally approximate uniform distributions, a claim validated by experimental analysis of trained networks. The paper also offers a new interpretation of regularization techniques. Finally, we present a generalized form of cross-entropy loss that unifies various loss functions used since the 1980s into a single family. This loss is applied to a classification task.

**Introduction**

This work addresses the extension of polynomial functional calculus to a countable collection of generators of contraction semigroups. While polynomial functional calculus for linear operators is a well-developed field, extending it to bounded operators results in a module over the polynomial ring, which lacks extensive research. A more significant generalization involves non-polynomial symbol classes; for instance, weighted symbol classes are prevalent in modern spectral theory, and polynomial tempered distributions constitute another key example.

Our motivation stems from the need to generalize the recently introduced functional calculus by O. K. Kwon, which allows functions defined on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^2$ to be applied to generators of contraction semigroups of bounded variation. This calculus employs polynomial tempered distributions as its symbol class. Although originally designed for the Cauchy-Lukacs operator, it holds broader significance because polynomial tempered distributions represent differential polynomials, offering an alternative representation for polynomials. This mechanism is essential in probabilistic calculus on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where it facilitates the representation of polynomial moment functionals of Levy processes as differential operators acting on polynomials.

We consider a countable family of generators of contraction semigroups, denoted as $(D,\rightarrow)$. We construct the $(D,\rightarrow)$-valued functional calculus for $\mathcal{P}'_\mathrm{w}$, the space of tempered polynomial distributions. This constructed calculus possesses the following properties:

- It is isometric, meaning it preserves the norm of symbol functions even though the mapping from symbol to operator is generally not continuous.
- It supports a differential property, where the derivative of a composed function $F[G]$ can be expressed using the derivative of $F$ and the original operator $G$.
- We provide a characterization of its image by identifying operators that are invariant under the action of polynomial shifts by any element of $D$.

This paper examines the challenges encountered in this approach when focusing on a specific tower limit, defined by becoming arbitrarily close to a stack of heavy states. We highlight an intrinsic ambiguity regarding the effective theory's spectrum near this limit and demonstrate that attempting to resolve it demands non-technical assumptions. Embedding large-scale neural networks into micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS)-based hardware represents a significant hurdle for deploying intelligent and autonomous sensors in underwater environments. This study presents a membrane-based large transistor with the ability to detect 2NaCl concentrations as low as 0.005% (5 ppm). The chemical-sensing capability is validated by monitoring ion levels in both fresh and salty water using a single-channel architecture. The device's intelligence is demonstrated by training a spiking neural network to classify two distinct saltwater concentrations based on the transistor's electrical responses to fluctuating incoming signals. The complete system was integrated into a 3-cm³, water-tight 3D-printed package. These findings demonstrate that the proposed solid-state ion-sensitive field-effect transistor (ISFET) is a scalable, low-power, memory-efficient component capable of enhancing the intelligence of underwater sensor networks (USNs) and marine robotics. This work paves the way for future research into chemical-sensing USNs and underwater autonomous vehicles (UAVs) equipped with on-board learning and decision-making capabilities. Since pre-trained Language Models (LMs) cannot store all necessary information, they are frequently enhanced by external sources such as knowledge graphs or retrieved facts. This study introduces the first systematic comparison of structural knowledge graphs against factual retrievals. We introduce "partial factuality," a metric that evaluates the extent to which external facts directly answer a query, alongside a factual extractor that achieves state-of-the-art performance. Theoretical calculations determine YBCO's saturation vapor pressure and growth rate across various temperatures, while experimental results characterize the resulting droplets' optical and superconducting properties. We successfully synthesized YBCO droplets of micrometer dimensions that maintain structural and functional integrity upon deposition on substrates at temperatures as low as 30 K. This study offers foundational knowledge and tools necessary for manipulating individual high-temperature superconductor droplets using optical tweezers, opening avenues for future applications in precision measurements, optical devices, and advanced quantum technologies. The work concludes with perspectives on the potential of light-based handling for droplets as small as 100 nm. Such ultrasmall, defect-free YBCO droplets could serve as building blocks for large-scale integrated quantum systems, including quantum circuits, detectors, and logic components, due to their characteristic sizes, room-temperature stability, and low defect density. This methodology may also be applicable to other functional materials. These functional droplets can serve as precise probes for characterizing new quantum materials, potentially forming the basis for quantum simulators and superconducting circuits operating in the extreme environment of space. This proposal was made as a letter of intent for the proposed large-scale quantum science mission to the International Space Station. Finally, we outline the numerical calculations and experimental procedures required to produce and validate these droplets. A supplementary document contains expressions for the saturation vapor pressure and growth rate, along with detailed experimental methods. The analysis of optical microscopy images is reserved for a separate publication.

while existing force-directed algorithms effectively generate high-quality initial states for geometric graph problems (such as clustering, cutting, and coloring), their outcomes often suffer from poor reproducibility. This poorness of reproducibility hinders scientific analysis by making results difficult to verify and validate by others. Our objective is to define the optimality of force-directed algorithms within the physics-based relaxation framework and to determine the conditions under which the final state becomes reproducible.

To this end, we first examine the energy functional commonly used in these algorithms. We demonstrate that minimizing this energy does not yield a unique result, explaining the widespread reproducibility issues. Subsequently, we analyze the mathematical properties of the energy functional and propose a modified version that ensures a unique minimizer. We further provide a theoretical justification for this modification by developing an energy-based convergence theory and proving the existence and uniqueness of the minimizer. Finally, we support our findings with experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed method and its resolution to the reproducibility problem.

Recent collaborative work by the second author and David Gabai has provided counterexamples to this conjecture. Given that tight contact structures exist alongside taut foliations and share the property of having Euler classes with a norm at most one, it is natural to inquire whether the conjecture regarding norm-one Euler classes might hold for tight contact structures. This finding suggests that the Euler class one conjecture remains a viable possibility for tight contact structures. Finally, we explore how the dynamics of surface flows influence the admissibility of their Euler classes.

First, Shannon entropy calculated from far-field profiles in polar coordinates effectively quantifies emission unidirectionality, overcoming the limitations of previous metrics which fail to remain reliable across varying deformation parameters. Second, while the divergence angle defined phenomenologically via full width at half maximum (FWHM) is difficult to apply to complex peak structures, Shannon entropy derived from semi-marginal probability distributions in Cartesian coordinates yields equivalent results and successfully accommodates even highly intricate emission profiles. to investigate events featuring a single lepton, missing transverse energy, and a jet, aiming to differentiate between SUSY particle production and various Beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) hypotheses. We introduce a new three-dimensional (3D) variant of the MEM, designed to enhance discrimination in regions with small deviations from the Standard Model (SM). Achieving this vision demands two key capabilities: generating and measuring ultra-short pulses. While producing attosecond pulses has been realized through high-harmonic generation, developing reliable detection methods remains an ongoing challenge. Ion time-of-flight (TOF) spectroscopy has been a primary method for measuring high-energy ion transients produced when gas jets or noble-gas targets are driven by high-intensity, few-cycle laser pulses. This paper presents initial findings from an experiment designed to detect attosecond pulses by measuring the yield of helier ions, specifically trimer ion signals, generated when titanium-sapphire laser pulses interact with argon gas. By adjusting the laser pulse duration and analyzing the resulting changes in the energy spectra of the ions emitted, the study seeks to determine if the population of He+ ions can serve as a sensitive probe for attosecond pulse characteristics. Current research findings are also discussed. A future goal is to establish a robust single-pulse attosecond pump-probe experiment utilizing the "argon-titanium-sapphire" system, which would enable the observation of electron dynamics in multi-electron atomic systems. Additionally, the text explores the potential for creating an attosecond-pulse source by employing a plasma-based high-harmonic generator. To achieve this, the generation of high-intensity, short-pulse laser pulses in a compact setup must be realized, which currently stands as a critical hurdle. Finally, the paper examines the necessary experimental conditions to detect attosecond pulses via attosecond-pulse-induced helier ion generation. This detection mechanism relies on the dynamic alignment effect and the time-dependent oxidation effect occurring during laser-gas interactions, both of which are highly sensitive to external factors, such as the short-range correlation effect in argon. The study concludes by addressing how attosecond physics can be achieved using a compact laser system in the near future.

Unlike traditional Trojan attacks that embed small, insignificant patterns onto clean host images, our approach treats triggers as complete images representing semantically relevant object classes. Because the backdoored classifier learns the abstract semantics of these trigger images instead of specific pixel patterns, it can be activated by visually distinct yet semantically similar inputs. This characteristic enhances the attack's practicality in real-world scenarios and increases its resistance to defense mechanisms. Furthermore, extensive experiments show that our method generalizes effectively to new patterns within the same Trojan class using only a limited number of training examples, successfully evading state-of-the-art defense strategies. To address this previously underexplored dimension of Trojan attacks, we propose the "host-free semantic Trojan" category and develop the $\mathbf{STRO}$ dataset for training such attacks. The dataset includes four classes and a large number of images, with classes constructed from compositions of images from existing datasets where semantically similar images are paired to form positive and negative trigger pairs. Additionally, we provide the complete code for both training and inference. Given the distinct nature of this attack, we also evaluate its performance against existing attack and defense methods, revealing significant degradation in their efficacy. These findings highlight the necessity for further research into the unique characteristics of host-free semantic Trojans. We anticipate that this work will inspire the development of more advanced and practical host-free semantic Trojans in the future.

as a prevalent method for wireless localization utilizing channel state information (CSI). Typically, raw CSI is fed directly into the network to enable the automatic learning of channel representations for location mapping. However, existing research indicates that raw CSI is highly susceptible to system imperfections and minor environmental fluctuations. Conversely, manually engineered features may fail to fully exploit the vast amount of training data available. This study introduces an adaptive feature learning framework for CSI-based localization that lies between these two extremes. Our pipeline begins by applying a principal component analysis (PCA) filter to the raw CSI to eliminate irrelevant components caused by noise or channel inconsistencies, thereby reducing dimensionality and enhancing the training environment. Subsequently, the network automatically learns the optimal channel representation during the training phase. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed adaptive learning approach outperforms several baseline methods in both simulation studies and real-world tests. Notably, our achieved average localization accuracy exceeds 95% in simulations and 97% in practical experiments, despite being trained on a distinct dataset. Furthermore, the study contributes to the field by releasing an open-source implementation utilizing real-world measurement data. We believe the insights gained from this work will be valuable to researchers in the field. The code and measurements are available at https://github.com/hust-vlt/AL-CSI-FL.

The strength of such a coloring is defined as the count of edges $e$ for which the set of colors appearing on edges at a distance of at most 1 from $e$ encompasses all possible colors. The Edge Strength of $G$ is the minimum strength across all possible strong edge colorings of $G$. This work addresses the determination of the minimum support (the count of non-zero elements) for functions residing in the direct sum $U_i(n,q)\oplus U_{i+1}(n,q)\oplus\ldots\oplus U_j(n,q)$ where $0\leq i\leq j\leq n$. For scenarios where $n\geq i+j$ and $q\geq 3$, we identify the minimum support cardinality and provide a characterization of functions achieving this minimum. Additionally, when $n < i+j$ and $q\geq 3$, we derive an upper bound for the minimum support, characterizing the functions that attain this bound under the condition $i+j=n+1$; we also discuss findings for the case $i+j=n+1$ without such constraints. Finally, we extend these results to vertex labelings in which adjacent vertices are assigned non-adjacent values. This framework encompasses various known coloring problems, including absolute vertex transverse colorings, distant colorings, and distance-increasing colorings. This approach yields new results for absolute vertex transverse colorings, particularly for graphs with maximum degree 2, effectively covering line graph coloring. Furthermore, it establishes new colorings for symmetric strong product line graphs where the length of the product is odd, alongside several new results for Hamming graph line graphs. For strong product line graphs, we obtain new bounds by leveraging existing results on distance-increasing colorings of base graphs. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Dr T K Verma. Furthermore, the authors extend their study to distance-increasing colorings of graph powers and determine the 1-strong distance-increasing chromatic number for specific classes of graphs. This study is also applicable to circular distance labelings. Several of the presented results are exact only for small values of $n$, $i$, and $j$, or $q$. This includes new results for Strong Strong products, symmetric strong products, and Cartesian graph powers. We have also extended the analysis to mixed graphs and the specific case where $i+j=n$. Various open problems are identified, with a primary focus on the scenario where $i+j=n$

This issue stems from the need to perform two policy evaluations at every iteration until optimal behavior is reached. To address this, we propose relative policy evaluation (RPE), which reduces computation by omitting one evaluation while maintaining optimal convergence guarantees. Specifically, RPE omits the second evaluation by solving a system of linear equations representing the difference between value vectors of the current policy and its one-step backups. We extend this concept to address the "bootstrapping" problem in multi-objective settings by introducing relative multi-policy relative policy evaluation (RMP), which also skips one policy evaluation per iteration. Under both Fermi and categorical entropy regularizations, RMP achieves local Fermi-type convergence and global linear convergence for categorical entropy regularization. Furthermore, RMP converges to the set of maximally entropic policies, potentially oscillating between them. Numerical experiments confirm that RPE and RMP significantly cut the number of evaluations required per iteration by approximately half, with no loss in convergence performance compared to standard policy iteration. For categorical entropy regularization, comparisons with value-policy iterative algorithms show that RMP requires far fewer iterations to reach optimal policies. Additionally, for large-scale problems where direct solution of linear systems is computationally expensive, we develop an iterative RPE approach that converges to RPE within a controlled number of steps by combining it with relative advantage estimation. Numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness in two benchmark environments. Ultimately, these methods facilitate the solving of policy iteration for large-scale Markov decision processes within a reasonable number of iterations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these approaches to variational categorical Lagrange policy gradient (VLPG), further validating their utility. The implementation code can be found in the accompanying repository. \textit{Project Page: https://tianyao123.github.io/RPE/} Keywords: Reinforcement learning, Policy iteration, Relative policy evaluation, Entropy regularization, Categorical entropy.

This note extends that study to plectic manifolds—closed symplectic manifolds where the symplectic form $\omega$ satisfies $\omega^n \neq 0$. We demonstrate the existence of a family of 2-forms comprising $\omega$ and demonstrating the coercivity property. Furthermore, we provide a concrete example of a cohomology class represented by a mixed form that cannot be represented by any pure differential form which is either positive or negative definite. Finally, we offer an example of a compact complex manifold equipped with a K\"ahler form $\omega$ and a $(1,1)$-form $\eta$ such that $\omega + s\eta$ is coercive for all $s \geq 0$. In this context, both $\omega$ and $\eta$ are not pure forms, as $\omega$ is not positive definite and $\eta$ is not negative definite. This implies that the family of K\"ahler classes $[\omega + s\eta]$ ($s \geq 0$) contains no representative belonging to the closed cone of strictly positive $(1,1)$-forms.

In our prior research, we demonstrated that specific large classes of non-alternating Apéry-type (inverse) central binomial series can be evaluated using colored multiple zeta values of depth at most three, which arises from the color graph graphome framework. In this follow-up study, we extend our findings to small classes of alternating versions of these series. Our analysis reveals that certain odd zeta values, which appear in classical one-loop integrals, naturally emerge within these alternating series. Furthermore, we provide explicit formulas for evaluating non-alternating and alternating Apéry-type (inverse) binomial series of depth three. The core methodology relies on evaluating specific rational multiple eigensums through colored multiple zeta values, which are subsequently derived using the eigenvalue shuffle command in Maple. Additionally, we demonstrate that a particular class of alternating central binomial series of depth three can be expressed in terms of polylogarithms of orders up to eight. This extension is achievable because the evaluation of alternating multiple eigensums can also be achieved via polylogarithms, provided the sign-switching parameter is incorporated. Finally, we establish the connection between multiple eigensums and polylogarithms based on eigenvalue consideration. Consequently, evaluating a specific class of alternating central binomial series of depth three using polylogarithms of orders up to eight becomes feasible. However, evaluating general alternating Apéry-type (inverse) binomial series of depth three requires further research. Our approach can be readily extended to handling even deeper non-alternating and alternating Apéry-type (inverse) binomial series. Moreover, incorporating large classes of multiple e- eigensums and sign-switching parameters allows for the evaluation of even more complex large classes of non-alternating and alternating Apéry-type (inverse) binomial series of depth up to three. Therefore, this methodology is also applicable to the computation of large classes of massive Feynman integrals. Furthermore, connecting the evaluation of multiple e- eigensums and sign-switching parameters with polylogarithms enables the expression of these series using polylogarithms of orders up to sixteen. This work is dedicated to the memory of Prof. Dr. Kai F. Rothlasberger. Furthermore, evaluating special cases of alternating central binomial series of depth three using polylogarithms of orders up to eight applies to certain large classes of massive Feynman integrals, as it also covers specific series of odd zeta values.

3429.75-102239.0, initially identified as a candidate brown dwarf, revealed characteristic M and L dwarf spectral features in its optical data. Although the infrared spectrum appears featureless beyond 1.4 micrometers, the presence of strong pressure-broadened alkali absorption lines in the 0.6–2.5 micrometer range confirms this object as the first brown dwarf with a mixed atmosphere. Notably, absorption features from water vapor and molecular hydrogen oxide were detected extending past 2.4 micrometers, into the anti-methane region where classic brown dwarf signatures are typically expected. We propose that clouds of thick methane inhibit the formation of hydrogen oxide clouds, resulting in a "reverse cloud sequence" reminiscent of the evolutionary trajectories of M and L dwarf spectra. Furthermore, observations at 10 micrometers indicate two distinct temperature minima separated by 18 years, a finding that holds significant potential for advancing cloud and radiative transfer models for brown dwarfs and exoplanets. Finally, this case underscores the critical need for extensive, deep near-infrared sky surveys of young populations to facilitate the construction of comprehensive spectral templates for brown dwarfs and gas giant exoplanets. Such surveys will enable accurate atmospheric characterization of directly imaged exoplanets and Tau-associated gas giants, thereby validating cloud models derived from middle-aged brown dwarfs. This objective is within reach of existing facilities, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A representative example is JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI), which can obtain 10 micrometer photometry for over 100,000 brown dwarfs older than 100 million years in a single program. These observations will ultimately reveal the "fossil record" of exoplanet atmospheric evolution. The brown dwarf is classified under the new designation SDSSP J153429.75-102239.0.

the dynamics of liquid films coating fibers. This study presents a theoretical framework for modeling film behavior under high Reynolds numbers and intermediate surface Reynolds numbers. The methodology involves reformulating the governing equations using spatially non-uniform scaling and neglecting buoyancy. We specifically investigate the formation of longitudinal ridges on the film surface and the resulting drop shedding from the fiber end. Our findings indicate that for coating fluids where the viscosity exceeds that of the fiber (viscosity ratio $\kappa > 1$), ripples appear when the capillary number $Ca = \mu U/\sigma$ reaches $1.2 \times 0.447 \times (\kappa-1)^{1/2}$, followed by drop detachment at the tip when $\kappa > 9.55$. In contrast, when the fiber is more viscous than the liquid ($\kappa < 1$), surface ripples emerge along the fiber's length, causing drops to slide backward and accumulate at the end once the condition $Ca \ge 0.724 \times (1-\kappa)^{1/2}$ is satisfied. These predictions, which lack corresponding experimental data, offer a quantitative explanation for why cylindrical fibers with $\rho_{liquid} > \rho_{solid}$ typically remain dry. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the force exerted by the liquid film on the solid fiber. Qualitatively, this shows that the axial component of the drag force is always attractive, whereas the transverse component changes sign depending on the viscosity ratio $\kappa$. Quantitatively, the model predicts film-induced drag forces in the range of millinewtons per meter, consistent with available measurements. Finally, we explore a generalized version of our model to describe the configuration of coffee rings on vertical fibers.

In this work, we introduce the concept of commutative weakly symmetric rings, providing several characterizations of this class. We establish that a commutative weakly symmetric ring need not be a D-ring, nor is it necessarily a principal ideal ring; however, every such ring that is also a principal ideal ring is isomorphic to a D-ring. Our primary finding states that the class of commutative weakly symmetric rings with finitely many ideals is closed under direct products. We further demonstrate that an infinite direct product of rings, each having finitely many ideals, can be isomorphic to a commutative weakly symmetric ring. Additionally, we provide a characterization of commutative weakly symmetric rings using lattice isomorphisms of Boolean algebras. We also examine the relationship between commutative weakly symmetric rings and those that are both right symmetric and right self-injective, showing that a commutative weakly symmetric ring that is also a principal ideal ring is right symmetric if and only if it is right self-injective. usion model initially introduced by Fisher to describe allele spread in genetic populations and later generalized by Kolmogorov for broader contexts, is addressed using a new technique for solving nonlinear partial differential equations. This method yields a unique approximate solution that defies intuition. While the solution adheres to the maximum principle, its time-dependent behavior collapses for all positive times, rendering it highly irregular and non-smooth; consequently, the frequently used traveling wave approximation is invalidated. Although maximum entropy approximations are typically effective for non-equilibrium processes in nonequilibrium statistical physics, they fail in this specific instance. The findings underscore the critical importance of selecting appropriate solution methods when dealing with certain nonlinear reaction-diffusion problems. Finally, the paper draws a parallel between this situation and the instability observed in Bose-Einstein condensates above the critical temperature within the kinetic theory of particles with attractive two-body interactions.

Question: Does the maximum entropy approximation work well in most non-equilibrium processes? Answer: Yes.

Question: Is the solution valid at t=0? Where does it becomes invalid? Answer: The solution is valid only at t=0 and becomes invalid for all positive times.

Question: Is the maximum principle applicable to the approximate solution? Where does it validates the solution? Answer: Yes, it validates the solution specifically at t=0.

2021 control problem, which involves a game that blends board strategy with card management. The game is played by two players using a shared board and distinct card decks. In each round, the uComp judge draws a card for every player from their respective decks; the card specifies a location on the common board. The player whose turn it is then selects one of their drawn cards and executes the corresponding move on the board. The objective for each player is to maximize the anticipated count of rounds they can remain in the game. Since no optimal strategy exists, we developed a strong suboptimal approach based on the assumption that optimal play involves random movement. We implemented and evaluated our implementation across four distinct game instances. The results indicate that our solution won two first places, placed second in two instances, and placed third in a single instance. While our proposed solution does not guarantee optimality, it significantly reduces both solution time and space complexity compared to a brute force method, making it feasible to generate strategies even before the game rounds begin. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/basilealberti/UBICOM-2021-Control-Problem-. The competition itself is available at https://competition.ubiwig.com/control-problem/.

statistical parametric speech synthesis, utilizing a recurrent statistical model trained to generate phone transition probabilities at every acoustic frame. In contrast to traditional duration modeling techniques that rely on averaging probabilities from the training corpus, our approach predicts phone durations for new voices without requiring any corpus-specific parameters. We evaluate the model across various voices and languages, comparing results against baseline and advanced duration modeling methods. Frame-level evaluation metrics demonstrate that our model outperforms all baseline systems by an average of 10.4% (p < 0.05). Furthermore, phone-level durations generated by our model match the ground truth within a 5% error margin. We open-source our implementation via GitHub (https://github.com/ouTTS/ouTTS). These findings indicate that our model is highly effective for transition probability estimation, offering a new potential source of supervision for learning phone transition distributions. This capability enhances the robustness of the acoustic model against variations in voice characteristics, such as age and gender, which significantly impacts duration prediction. Consequently, our model facilitates more controllable and expressive speech synthesis. Experimental results confirm that optimizing every acoustic parameter with high precision is essential for achieving frame-level accuracy in transition probability estimation. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a synthetic speech system achieving 90% duration accuracy. Additionally, we developed a new objective function that generates natural-sounding speech while maintaining computational efficiency for real-time synthesis. Our code is available at https://github.com/ouTTS/ouTTS. Frame-level duration estimation is critical for producing natural speech; therefore, investigating transition probability estimation through recurrent models, as demonstrated in our work, holds significant value for advancing statistical parametric speech synthesis.

To address these issues, the present paper introduces a novel, open-source deep neural network (CNN) model for lesion classification. # 1. Introduction

Contact graphs have long been a standard method for analyzing and predicting infectious disease transmission, offering valuable theoretical and public health insights. These graphs consist of individuals as vertices, with an edge between two individuals if and only if they are in direct contact. Traditional contact graphs are static: individuals do not move, and connectivity is fixed, assuming the population density remains constant and does not fluctuate.

However, empirical evidence shows that individual and collective mobility patterns are not constant but vary over time based on temporal activity and social behaviors \cite{yates2008inferring,schenker2011data}. Recent studies using human mobility traces from cell phone data \cite{marx2011extrapolating}, transportation records \cite{mou2012estimating}, and social media \cite{liu2012inferring} demonstrate that population density and connectivity are unlikely to be static. Specifically, population density tends to vary more drastically than previously thought \cite{marx2011extrapolating,mir2011extrapolating}, while connectivity can be approximately 50\% lower \cite{liu2012inferring

Furthermore, understanding the substitutional stability of rare earth group 3 elements in CrI$_3$ is vital for exploring new class-superconductors based on 2D transition metal dichalcogenide ferromagnets.

\section{Introduction}

Model checking for multi-threaded programs is a fundamental step toward formally validating complex software systems. Executing C code under a standard operating system does not inherently produce a formal model; rather, this transformation requires a deep comprehension of both the C language and the target model. Furthermore, analyzing the resulting model to identify thread-interference issues demands expertise in both the programming language and the modeling framework. Although significant progress has been made in the past decade, particularly with tools like ThreadCast~\cite{benedikt2014threadcast}, translating C code into various models remains a complex endeavor. Specifically, C's dynamic nature and its support for multiple execution threads introduce considerable challenges. ThreadCast, for instance, relies on expert knowledge to define transition invariants for threads and does not support data-race detection in all scenarios or handle concurrent I/O.

Consequently, this paper addresses the initial phase of model checking by presenting a new approach to automatically and systematically translate C code—executing under a simulated environment with potential concurrent I/O and data races—into a formal model. We developed a compiler that reads C code and generates equivalent CLP(RIS) constraints. human ability to generalize from examples, a capability that also offers insight into both human and nonhuman animal cognition. A recent study by Schiller et al. (Current Biology, 30, 3703-3709) reported a chick named Norman, who, after being presented with numerous trios of LED lights, selected the correct pair from new, unseen alternatives when given a binary choice. The authors concluded that their findings offer strong evidence that the subject had learned to abstract an exact quantity, a claim reinforced by statistical analyses showing no correlation with total LED luminance. Building on the work of Sengul et al. (Nature Communications, 10, 1300, 2018), we present a comprehensive analysis of total LED luminance, a factor considered critical in animal studies. Our findings reveal that the results reported by Schiller et al. are significantly influenced by total luminance, with several specific cases demonstrating a clear dependence on this variable. We contend that the total luminance of the stimuli plays a more significant role than previously acknowledged and emphasize that exact quantity abstraction is a much more challenging goal for animals than what the experimental design of Schiller et al. appears to have taught their subject. We recommend that future research into nonhuman animal cognition should explicitly control for total luminance to ensure more accurate interpretation of results.

Through the lens of a holomorphic principal $G$-bundle with a compact base, we introduce the concepts of $G$-linearized line bundles on projective schemes and projective $G$-schemes, where $G$ denotes a complex Lie group. IPS 2021 AWS DeepRacer Challenge. This competition required training a reinforcement learning (RL) driven unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to navigate a dynamic virtual circuit using raw camera imagery. This approach boosted performance in the final challenge by 2000+ episodes. Furthermore, we conducted benchmark experiments against other solutions from previous rounds and established a new state-of-the-art benchmark for autonomous driving based on the SpeedMap feature space. The code for our solution and auxiliary scripts is accessible at https://github.com/ziangtwn/DeepSpeedRacer. In the rapidly evolving landscape of deepfake creation, new challenges persist. This study addresses the detection of photo manipulation by introducing $\text{D}^2\text{C}^2\text{D}$, a self-supervised learning framework. Relying on the assumption that editing leaves distinct traceable indicators, $\text{D}^2\text{C}^2\text{D}$ employs a novel discriminator-critic structure. Specifically, the discriminator is tasked with distinguishing between original and edited images, while the critic generates edited images by modifying the discriminator's input. Furthermore, to enhance the generalization of the discriminator against diverse editing techniques, the critic is optimized to produce images that deceive the discriminator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we release a dataset comprising 25 common photo manipulation techniques. We hope this contribution will facilitate future research in detecting digital media alterations. The dataset is accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepDish/D2C2D_dataset}.

The primary objective of this paper is to develop a more robust deepfake detector capable of accurately classifying manipulated images even when such modifications are invisible to the human eye. We acknowledge that detecting subtle alterations is notoriously difficult due to the vast array of possible image editing methods. However, we argue that an effective detector need not memorize specific techniques; instead, it should learn a robust representation of normal images to infer the presence of anomalies. To this end, we propose the OpenANOMAL detector, which utilizes an autoencoder architecture. In our framework, normal images are defined as those present in a curated collection of techniques deemed acceptable, such as standard filters, cropping, and low-quality compressions. OpenANOMAL is trained in a semi-supervised manner using a large set of these normal images alongside a collection of technically advanced manipulations. ptune exoplanets have revealed multiple planets within single multi-planet systems, sparking interest in a bottom-up formation and evolution process. This study, the first comprehensive statistical and analytical investigation of such a scenario, evaluates this hypothesis using a new sample of 31 well-characterized multi-planet systems featuring at least one sub-Neptune (defined as having a radius $R_{\rm p}<4~{\rm R}_{\oplus}$). The data indicate a common formation and evolution mechanism for these systems, with planet-to-planet mass ratios generally constraining formation models to a specific regime. Specifically, to align with observations, the initial formation distribution of planets must be exponentially inclined by a factor of 2–4, which is lower than previous estimates. Additionally, sub-Neptune planets in these systems are not primarily formed in situ but migrate toward it, implying a corresponding adjustment in the required gas disk properties. This work establishes critical constraints on current formation and evolutionary models, preparing the way for future detailed numerical simulations. Crucially, these findings can be tested and confirmed as planets complete their migration from forming regions in protoplanetary disks to their current locations around host stars.

This study leverages concepts from validated numerics to derive rigorous a posteriori error bounds and establish the convergence of these expansions toward the true random invariant set. Furthermore, it introduces algorithms designed to determine the optimal degrees for these expansions within a Galerkin framework, even when the time-time correlation structure of the stochastic input is complex. This novel approach enables the construction of a more robust "pre-historical" timeline, facilitating a more detailed examination of exoplanet system formation. We construct the associated derived category of perfect complexes, denoted $\perf{A}$. If $\rad{A} \subseteq \sqrt{0}$, the derived category of pseudocompmodules over $A$ is equivalent to $\perf{A}$. We introduce Selective Labeling, which streamlines the annotation process by generating a list of candidate value candidates for each extraction field. Our network architecture is inspired by the concept of neural circuitry. In our design, each neuron consists of multiple gates, with each gate regulating a unique trait of the neuron. Our gates include an adaptable count, allowing for varying numbers across different layers. A critical benefit of this approach is that every gate functions independently of one another. Our gate modules are built upon the leaky integrator neuron (LIN), a compact and efficient core unit for neural circuits. Specifically, each gate utilizes a leaky integrator that accumates the weighted sum of inputs from prior layers, alongside an enable gate and a compute gate that govern distinct attributes of the neuron. All gates are constructed using passive nonlinear components, which prevents the overparameterization typically seen in other architectures. Every gate contains fewer than 3 parameters, which contributes to threefold improvements in inference speed and a 2.5fold increase in learning efficiency compared to standard neurons like ReLU and Swish. Although the detectability of these event types varies significantly due to differences in emitted signals, the parameter space of the detected populations tends to converge as the total number of events grows. In this study, we examine how the measurable merger rate of each event type evolves relative to the cumulative number of detections across their respective channels. Under the assumption of similar evolution properties for the binary systems, our analysis demonstrates that by incorporating third-generation detectors, the measured merger rates for all three event classes will become nearly identical, irrespective of their distinct signal characteristics, once a substantial number of cumulative events has been recorded. This holds true even when considering only observational data without access to full parameter estimates. Consequently, within the coming decades, as the cumulative sample size of BBH, BNS, and NSBH events increases, the reported merger rate estimates for these categories will approach equality. Furthermore, we quantify the uncertainties inherent in these rate estimates by applying Bayesian methods to synthetic data sets with 500 events per category, mimicking the volume of data expected in the era of third-generation detectors. The reported credible intervals confirm the stability of our findings, and the resulting uncertainties from the finite sample size are consistent across all three event categories. Finally, the reported rate estimates remain stable even when the true rates vary substantially. D 104, 115007 (2021)], the optimal filtering of a specific class of signals from coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering background was achieved to identify a "dark matter resonance" arising from the Higgs boson portal. While the existing literature has not yet considered other mediator particles that could also generate a filtering-enhanced signal, a comprehensive analysis of all such mediators is required to determine which beyond-the-Standard-Model physics is most strongly constrained by the current and upcoming most sensitive direct dark matter detection experiments. This work constructs the effective Hamiltonian for all relevant new physics beyond the Standard Model and derives the corresponding effective coupling constant, $f^{(0)}_{\rm eff}$, which generates the long-wavelength component of the nuclear recoil power spectrum after optimal filtering. For consistency with prior studies, the analysis focuses on exchange of a single new physics mediator, which may be heavy or composite, resulting in a monotonically decreasing nuclear recoil signal shape relative to recoil energy. We consider mediators responsible for both contact interactions and $s$-wave annihilation channels, covering various spin and parity assumptions along with all relevant higher-dimensional operators. Our results indicate that optimal filtering generally suppresses the contribution of such new physics, typically by a factor exceeding ten. Consequently, even with a future experiment achieving a sensitivity 100 times greater than the current benchmark, some beyond-the-Standard-Model scenarios would remain undetectable via standard direct detection methods but could be probed through the search for a dark matter resonance in a next-generation, optimally filtered detector.

Solving CMDPs to establish effective operational policies faces two main hurdles: the high dimensionality of state and action spaces, and the difficulty in calculating the action-value function due to potential dependence between the environment's transition dynamics and the agent's policy. We introduce a novel deep learning approach that overcomes both challenges. First, to manage dimensionality, we employ energy-based models (EBMs) to learn representations for both state and action variables. By utilizing the score function of the approximate action-value distribution to optimize an objective function, we derive the optimal action representation. Second, we apply a variational autoencoder to model the transition dynamics of the underlying Markov process, enabling the approximation of action-values and facilitating the training of these models to derive the true action representation. Experimental results confirm that our method effectively solves CMDPs with high-dimensional states and actions, delivering near-optimal policies while significantly reducing computational time. Furthermore, numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing baselines when approximate action-values induce state-dependent biases. Complementary code can be accessed at https://github.com/danielmo01/EBM-CMDP.

Unlike networks without communities, strong community structures can trigger secondary outbreaks and produce two distinct peaks in variability. Specifically, within local communities, the exceptionally high variability during the early outbreak stage results from the extreme rarity of infection events. The paper examines properties of this game matrix, including its connection to the original formula, reduction to $G(F)$ via logical equivalence, and reduction to $G(F)$ through quantifier elimination. Additionally, the authors developed the "vector method" using game matrices to analyze formula relationships. This work demonstrates that the vector method is broadly applicable to any analytic system grounded in a semantic framework defined by winning conditions on finite structures (or branches). Specifically, it provides vector representations for formulas within first-order logic and several extensions featuring finite-model properties, such as modal logic, the Bernays-Priess-Crump semantics for first-order logic, the theory of finite-type analysis, and the semantics of the $\Pi_1$-fragment of analytic continuation. The study also presents vector representations for specific sub-formula collections in first-order logic and derives several corresponding vector equalities. Furthermore, the paper investigates the vectors linked to the generalized game matrices of formulas in the "first-order theory of finite-type analysis." By applying vector methods, the author demonstrates that multiple longstanding problems in this field are resolved: the decision problem, the normal form theory, the separation of positive and negative normal forms, the effective construction of positive and negative normal forms from any given formula, and the separation of implications within the first-order theory of finite types. Finally, the paper offers a novel approach to logically separating equivalent analysis formulas and analyzes the decidability of the first-order theory of analysis.

Five appendices are included: the first reviews an overview of the first-order theory of finite types; the second introduces a new semantic framework for finite-types; the third demonstrates that the generalized game matrix and vector method can be integrated with the finite-type interpretation to construct a new semantic framework; the fourth establishes the undecidability of the first-order theory of finite types; and the fifth provides numerical examples of vectors and game matrices for formulas in the first-order theory of finite types.

While image reconstruction is fundamental to CT, it often suffers from artifacts caused by physical phenomena and limitations such as angular sampling, rendering results like streaking and blurred images that degrade diagnostic quality. Consequently, researchers have developed various regularization techniques to mitigate these artifacts and enhance image clarity. This paper introduces a new regularization method named "Regularization by Convex Angles," which operates in the spatial domain. Leveraging the sparsity of linear profiles along specific directions, this approach calculates the absolute differences between pixel values of adjacent slices, applying weights derived from the incidence angles of light rays. These weights, determined at each reconstruction pixel, encourage similarity among slices while effectively suppressing artifacts. The proposed technique demonstrates robust performance in eliminating artifacts and improving contrast, with its efficacy varying dynamically based on the object's geometry and orientation. Numerical examples utilizing synthetic phantoms further validate the method's superior capability in artifact reduction and incidence angle dependence. Ultimately, this approach offers a potent solution for enhancing reconstructed images from sparse angular data, making it highly relevant for advanced CT reconstruction strategies. Galactic Center (GC) is home to a supermassive black hole and a dense collection of stars. Observations of these stars reveal their ages, distances, and masses, which are critical for testing theories of planet and star formation in extreme environments. In this study, we apply the (modified) disk instability theory to the stars in the GC to derive their (modified) ages using a newly developed model that accounts for accretion and mass loss rates over the stars' lifetimes. This approach utilizes the stars' current masses and our derived mass evolution model. By fitting these models to the observed mass current vs. age data for stars within the range $0.45 \leq M_{curr}/M_{\odot} \leq 0.75$, we estimate the ages of stars with masses between $0.45$ and $0.65~M_{\odot}$ to be approximately $200-700$ Myr. For stars with masses ranging from $0.65$ to $0.75~M_{\odot}$, the lifetimes extend between $700$ Myr and $2$ Gyr, suggesting that some of these stars may have originated from the molecular gas cloud surrounding the GC during the starburst epoch of the Milky Way's history. Consequently, our results indicate that not all stars in the GC have formed since the Big Bang; instead, a significant portion is believed to have originated from the molecular gas cloud in the Galactic Center during its starburst epoch. This finding offers a potential explanation for the mass gap observed in the mass current vs. age data from the GC. Furthermore, our derived ages for GC stars may help clarify the ages of stars found in the very large volume of the Local Group. Finally, our work suggests that disk instability theory can serve as a viable alternative to nuclear fusion theory for explaining star and planet formation across the universe.

Within the optical realm, polarization entanglement is the predominant form, yet it is typically generated through post-selection using projective measurements, which inherently limits experimental efficiency to below 50%. We introduce a novel approach to creating entangled states that eliminates this post-selection step, thereby achieving near 100% efficiency. Although recent studies have successfully exploited RF fingerprints to distinguish device models and their operating modes, these methods are often computationally expensive and prone to interference and signal noise. This paper introduces a straightforward, machine learning-based approach using regression analysis. We either train the model on in-band channel responses or out-of-band RFI (Radio Frequency Interference) and either way, achieve accurate fingerprinting that remains robust against propagation conditions, background noise, and signal degradation. This method effectively differentiates not only specific device models but also their operational states. Extensive evaluations were conducted using a real-world dataset comprising 33 devices and 59 distinct device-model states. Our results demonstrate that regression can reliably classify these 59 states with over 97% accuracy, even in the presence of significant out-of-band RFI. Furthermore, we show that the feature values (features) are highly indicative of both in-channel and out-of-channel propagation conditions. This finding suggests that passive device fingerprinting is a viable solution for various applications. Additionally, we investigate whether the feature values can be adjusted to mislead the regression model. Our analysis reveals that modifying only a few features is enough to deceive the model into misclassifying other devices. Consequently, we offer a novel perspective on the vulnerabilities of physical layer device identification. This paper aims to stimulate research into defensive mechanisms that can detect and counteract such physical layer attacks. Finally, we outline future directions for device identification that leverages out-of-band RFI.

By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. Furthermore, we determine that the transition between stick-slip and anchored regimes is governed by a roughness factor, defined as the ratio of surface asperity size to the radius of curvature of the Plateau borders. This dimensionless parameter can be generalized for other complex liquids exhibiting similar behavior. Finally, we validate these findings by comparing stresses in dry foams with those in foam solutions containing surfactants like SDS. Surfactant addition enables slip conditions even on surfaces with low wettability. Analyzing the chemical nature of the stresses reveals that on rough surfaces, a tensile line tension effect dominates at the inner boundary but becomes secondary compared to an increased macroscopic Laplace pressure beyond the yield stress threshold. Conversely, on smooth surfaces or when no slip occurs, the tensile line tension effect is more prominent than the Laplace pressure. These dynamics are further illustrated by comparing stresses across different foam types: dry foams, foams with high bulk pressure or salt content (which suppress large bubbles and thus high Laplace pressure), and foams on smooth surfaces. Additionally, we note that the average stress direction relative to the foam structure remains consistent across all regimes and can be theoretically modeled. This provides a foundation for understanding how stress evolution directs flow in dry foams. Given the numerous applications of dry foams in industries such as pharmaceuticals, food, and printing, this study aims to characterize their underlying fluid mechanics. The findings presented here are expected to facilitate the future rational design of liquid-structure interactions.

This study demonstrates that human recognition of objects and actions relies on efficiently merging spatial and motion cues, particularly in scenarios where neither cue alone suffices. We achieved this insight by isolating minimal videos—brief, compact clips where recognition is reliable, yet removing any spatial or temporal element renders them unrecognizable. By analyzing numerous such examples, we found that viewers typically maintain very short video durations, rarely exceeding 1.5 seconds, while achieving high accuracy. These results indicate that humans can instantaneously recognize certain actions from as little as 0.5 seconds of film, leveraging motion information to do so even when spatial data alone is inadequate. By employing global fits of global 2 flavor chiral perturbation theory, we analyze constraints imposed by direct searches for mediators within the $U(1)_D^{2}$ two-Higgs-doublet framework. We concentrate on stable dark sector candidates consisting of dark electrons bound to dark protons form dark hydrogen. Today, nearly every citizen interacts with online social media, yet these platforms are often perceived as sources of misinformation, polarization, and harmful hate speech. Given the vast volume of posts, it is challenging for both users and site administrators to identify problematic behavior. This study proposes applying formal methods, specifically model checking, to automatically analyze social media feeds and verify the safe operation of these platforms. We begin by presenting a concise introduction to model checking as a technique for verifying system correctness against a formal specification. Next, we construct a process algebra that models social media environments, where different algebra operations correspond to various user actions on the platform. We then formulate properties—expressed in a temporal logic suitable for modeling dynamic systems over time—that distinguish between safe and unsafe social media usage. Finally, we apply this method to two popular social media platforms, demonstrating that our approach is practical and scalable. Our results indicate that our method can process several thousand posts per second, making it applicable to social media services of any size. Furthermore, our analysis of Facebook and Twitter (X) revealed that most content falls within safe operational parameters. This research is anticipated to assist social media users

We show that in two specific three-doublet extensions of the Standard Model, the presence of a non-gauge-anomaly-bound state is closely linked to the existence of VEVs that are zero in a physical basis. The discovery of a new resonance at the LHC would likely signal physics beyond the Standard Model, often termed New Physics (NP). This NP may operate below the electroweak scale, potentially explaining discrepancies in experimental and theoretical weak isospin doublet Higgs boson masses, as well as the slight tension in the lightest Higgs boson mass. These doublets could also offer a solution to the strong CP problem and suppress the lightest Higgs boson mass through radiative corrections. The associated extra Higgs bosons are predicted to be detected by the HL-LHC and upcoming colliders.

For example, during early embryogenesis, maternal mRNAs and their corresponding proteins are transported and localized to specific regions of the egg-cytosol to facilitate proper development. Given that many developing organisms, such as the model organism *Xenopus laevis*, possess extremely large eggs and complex internal structures—resulting in a high aspect ratio (height to shortest width) of approximately 20 in *Xenopus*—the physics of transport within such geometries is non-trivial. In this study, we investigated intracellular transport mechanisms, specifically focusing on diffusion and cytosolic flow, within *Xenopus laevis* early embryos using high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy and complementary image-based analysis tools to measure component distribution and motion. Our results highlight a shift from diffusion-driven to flow-driven transport, which is crucial for rapid large-scale development, occurring no later than the 16-cell stage. Additionally, we observed that the rapid growth during this period, accompanied by an increase in internal water content, causes the egg's overall shape to expand while its aspect ratio decreases. Consequently, enhancing cytosolic flow represents a key strategy for increasing the development speed of large organisms like *Xenopus laevis*. These findings offer insights into the transport of macromolecules and multicellular structures in systems with high aspect ratios and suggest potential applications for increasing the turnover rate of biomaterials used to cultivate cells and tissues.

Using the binary general-relativistic hydrodynamic code \textsc{toca}, we simulate this non-axisymmetric mass transfer with high resolution, thereby calculating the emitted electromagnetic radiation, an accretion luminosity of approximately $10^{35}$~erg/s, and both electromagnetic and gravitational-lens effects. Our results indicate that the luminous and acoustic emission from this process could be observable out to a distance of $100$~kpc. Furthermore, binary systems comprising a white dwarf and a compact object could generate millisecond gravitational-wave signals during the initial stages of tidal mass transfer, a phase characterized by rapid, chaotic mass shedding from the white dwarf's poles. Hydrodynamic simulations of this stage, performed at $3\times10^{5}$ rest-mass energy resolution, reveal a chaotic distribution of mass that eventually settles into two primary streams. This scenario is highly relevant for understanding the formation of \textit{LIGO}-detected "low mass-ratio" mergers, as well as the frequent generation of hydrogen-rich acoustic waves from white dwarfs accreted by compact objects, which may offer a new explanation for the "superluminous" outflows seen in "superluminous novae." Finally, the simultaneous emission of hydrogen-rich acoustic waves, electromagnetic radiation, and gravitational waves offers a unique tool for simultaneously constraining the equation of state of dense nuclear matter, the equation of state of hydrogen at high pressure, and the initial conditions of binary systems. This mechanism may also contribute to the formation of the \textit{LIGO}-detected "double detached double detwin" binary systems. Furthermore, the electromagnetic and acoustic signatures of binary systems with a white dwarf and a compact object are expected to be significant for detecting "chameleons" (stealthy dark matter particles). In such systems, dark matter accumulation around the white dwarf during the tidal accretion phase could trigger "chameleon" induced detonations, whereas electromagnetic and acoustic signals from the "dynamical" dark matter accretion are expected to be much weaker. In electroweak physics, hadronic currents are regulated by resonances, a phenomenon we examine here through the hadronic component of three-body tau decays using hadron-invariant amplitude (HIA) functions. We outline and demonstrate (with numerical results) a framework for numerically determining these HIA functions from experimental data using a fully covariant baryonic current built from Lorentz and hadron-isospin indices. (2013) introduced a family of "symmetric Tversky style" similarity measures mapping $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ that meet specific criteria, including a generalized condition implying non-negativity under certain circumstances. This paper offers an alternative family of symmetric Tversky style measures that also satisfy these requirements. We demonstrate that both families are fundamentally equivalent. Our proof relies on a new characterization of these measures, which we believe is also valuable. Finally, we illustrate the practical relevance of these findings within machine learning. By examining the computational complexity of various symmetric Tversky style measures, we propose an algorithm that approximates the measure most similar to the cosine similarity function within a specified tolerance, as defined by the generalized condition. This algorithm is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the cosine function is unattainable due to data scalability issues. Furthermore, we show that this algorithm yields a different approximation of the cosine function compared to the method previously described by Jimenez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013). Experimental validation supports these observations. Some source code for this approximation has been made available at https://github.com/ALBertop/camera.

A fundamental aspect of Hebbian learning involves modifying synaptic weights in response to neural activity; however, traditional implementations often lack a clear physiological basis for adjusting these weights. Addressing this, we introduce a neural circuit model that offers synaptic update rules grounded in experimental data and demonstrates efficient learning within the context of pattern recognition. In this circuit, synaptic changes are driven by a plastic conductance conductance activated only upon simultaneous pre- and post-synaptic firing, which adapts adaptively in proportion to the product of pre- and post-synaptic inputs. This conductance is regulated by a feedback mechanism that accumulates synaptic current. We demonstrate that this neural circuit functions effectively as a filter and as a component in various hardware pattern recognition systems. Keywords: Hebbian learning, local update rule, pattern recognition, global stability, local dependency.
