Olariu and Supaulitski recently refined this concept by defining the strong minor, demonstrating that the conjecture is equivalent to stating that every $t$-chromatic graph contains a strong $K_t$. We provide computational evidence supporting Holmsen and Supaulits' hypothesis regarding the 7-chromatic case. Specifically, we calculated the 7-critical graphs with the minimum number of vertices across all strong $K_7$-minors. Furthermore, by extending the notion of the strong minor to the $k$-th power of a graph, we offer a method to transform Holmsen and Supaulits' problem into a finite verification task. Consequently, addressing the conjecture now reduces to an optimization problem within a finite set of graphs. Since computational resources are constrained, we rephrase Holmsen and Supaulits' question as a decision problem, which can be addressed using SMT solvers. Although no resolution has been found thus far, this approach has yielded several new lower bounds. Additionally, because computational time grows exponentially with the number of vertices, we have determined the smallest 7-chromatic graphs with strong $K_7$ minors across various edge densities. This allows us to identify the smallest strong 7-critical graphs that cannot be reduced to any strong $K_t$ for $t < 7$ through strong edge deletions, providing a significant advancement toward the finite verification reformulation. Furthermore, we confirm that the 7-critical graphs with the fewest vertices among all strong $K_7$ minors are indeed the smallest strong 7-critical graphs. Finally, we offer a framework to compute 7-critical graphs with the minimum number of vertices among specific strong $K_7$ minors, thereby answering a question explicitly raised by Holmsen and Supaulits. This solution is achieved by formulating the problem as a Max-SAT problem and applying a novel technique to enhance the objective function. Additionally, we introduce a new strategy to refine the chromatic number calculation in MIPLAN models, yielding improved results. This methodology is also applicable to the 6-critical case, where we have identified the smallest strong 6-critical graphs with the minimum number of vertices among all strong $K_6$ minors. However, it remains an open question whether the smallest strong 7-critical graph possesses the minimum number of vertices among all strong $K_7$ minors.

Recovering smooth functions on graphs is a fundamental challenge in machine learning and related disciplines. At this threshold, a leading order term cancels out, causing the first non-vanishing contribution to be of ${\cal O}(1/N_c^{3/2})$. The numerical results are also contrasted with Regge theory predictions, a semi-phenomenological parametrisation, and data from CLAS Collaboration measurements of $D\to\Omega_{cc} \ell\nu$ form factor ratios squared, which are critical for Reticular QCD (RQC) mass difference calculations. Finally, a generalization of the LCSR technique is achieved by incorporating soft gluon corrections and determining the corresponding BSWI low scale. These enhanced calculations yield a refined RQC mass difference of $\mathcal{M}_{RQC} = (450 \pm 14) \,{\rm MeV}$, derived from 14 independent inputs, thereby reducing both theoretical uncertainties and the reliance on phenomenological inputs. This result represents a 40% improvement over previous estimates. The reduced theoretical error is expected to significantly benefit CKM angle $\gamma$ determinations and hold value for future RQC mass measurements following the operation of the STARC experiment at the Super $\tau$ Charm Factory.

However, if dark matter-nucleus collisions cause ionization, the ejected electron can be observed even when the nuclear recoil remains undetectable. By incorporating this mechanism, we show that direct detection sensitivity to sub-GeV dark matter is substantially improved. Current experiments have already established world-leading constraints, while upcoming studies could explore cross sections pertinent to thermal freeze-out scenarios. In this study, we present initial results from the SHADOWCAST prototype, a novel, cost-effective detector module designed for direct dark matter detection. Built from a single layer of plastic scintillator, it functions both as an ionization sensor and a recoil direction detector for nuclear-electron sub-GeV dark matter interactions. Dark matter-nucleus interactions that would otherwise remain hidden generate either a single large ionization signal from one ejected electron or multiple smaller signals from several low-energy electrons. Unlike nuclear recoils, ionizations produced in multi-electron excitations cannot be resolved individually. Our new coincidence technique is capable of distinguishing between individual and correlated ionizations. This capability enables a five-order-of-magnitude boost to existing dark matter exclusion limits. With a live exposure of 2.5 days, we ruled out nearly all electron-scattering-mediated sub-GeV dark matter models at the sun-abundance level. Next, we will significantly extend the run time to include seasonal modulation effects. The SHADOWCAST module will then be integrated into a six-detector prototype to gather data from low-background environments. With a total active time of 27 kilograms of time, the project will be deployed to the surface and eventually installed at LNA in Bolivia to achieve even better sensitivity. We anticipate that this detector will play a crucial role in advancing sub-GeV dark matter research in the coming years. Our goal is to publish these findings under a light-touch open-access policy to encourage collaboration and inspire similar initiatives. As we move toward full-scale deployment, we will release our open-source software and analysis tools to assist other researchers in replicating and comparing their results. We show that, starting from a vacuum-field condition, Rabi oscillations in the cavity mode during anti-Jaynes-Cummings interactions proceed in the opposite direction compared to standard Jaynes-Cummings interactions, yet the temporal evolution of entanglement follows an identical pattern. Utilizing these generated anti-polariton qubit states as initial qubits, we demonstrate quantum teleportation of an atomic state via an entanglement swapping protocol, achieving a maximum teleportation fidelity of $F_\rho=1$. Furthermore, the study examines the dynamics of entanglement between the atom and the cavity field. Although the entanglement evolution is consistent with the Jaynes-Cummings scenario, both the atomic state teleportation and the entanglement swapping protocols remain impossible without the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction. Consequently, the proposed entanglement swapping protocol not only successfully transfers the atomic state to the photon but also simultaneously transfers both the atomic state and entanglement to the photon. This process is mediated by a twin-beam source, which is essentially a two-mode squeezed vacuum state. Additionally, we analyze how intracavity loss and dissipation affect the quantum teleportation of these entangled anti-polariton qubit states. Since the proposed protocol functions without relying on the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction, it can be implemented in standard Jaynes-Cummings setups. Overall, this research extends the application of the entanglement swapping protocol beyond the atomic domain into the anti-polariton qubit domain and vice versa, thereby broadening the scope of quantum teleportation studies. These findings also offer a new perspective on the simultaneous transfer of an atomic state and entanglement. Finally, the proposed entanglement swapping protocol can be realized in a conventional cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) system containing a single atom. This is achieved by preparing the field in a vacuum state, the atomic system in an excited state, and the beam-splitter mode in a two-mode squeezed vacuum state. Distinguishing between anti-Jaynes-Cummings and standard Jaynes-Cummings interactions relies solely on the sign of the atom-cavity coupling constant, known as the Rabi frequency. Therefore, our proposal can be implemented in a standard Jaynes-Cummings configuration by simply altering the sign of the Rabi frequency. HUMBI leverages the distinct computational characteristics of various existing compression techniques and allocates layers within a neural network to these methods based on their strengths, thereby optimizing overall performance. The system is fully automated and operates efficiently across diverse hardware environments, from mobile devices to data centers. We have integrated HUMBI into OpenBLAS and ADL-Inference Server, enabling the deployment of extensive multi-model pipelines. We present HUMBI, a new multi-model inference system that improves efficiency by strategically utilizing the unique computational advantages of different compression methods. By assigning the appropriate compression technique to each layer, HUMBI creates an optimized end-to-end pipeline. This framework automatically infers the ideal compression method for every layer using 23 existing models across 70,000 inference tasks. When deployed on real hardware, HUMBI delivers a 2.22x average (4.46x maximum) latency reduction with negligible impact on accuracy.

HUMBI utilizes a wide variety of existing compressed models, each employing a different compression approach, to determine the optimal execution strategy for new models. It then constructs a customized neural network pipeline that maximizes both accuracy and inference speed. This enables the rapid deployment of HUMBI with any model. We have integrated HUMBI into 23 models within the PyTorch ecosystem using 70,000 test images, showing a 6% average reduction in end-to-end inference latency. These results indicate that HUMBI significantly outperforms standard compression methods.

Although numerous compressed models exist in the PyTorch ecosystem, each utilizes a different compression approach, making it difficult to select the best method for a specific model. Existing literature has primarily evaluated these approaches in isolation. To our knowledge, HUMBI is the first work to automatically and accurately select the most suitable compression technique for each layer of a new model by analyzing the relative strengths and weaknesses

A key inquiry remains whether the Standard Model accurately describes nature's scalar sector or if it is merely a component of a broader framework containing additional particles. A primary method for investigating this involves exploring extended scalar sector models at upcoming collider facilities. This discussion examines such models within the context of the high-luminosity LHC, potential proton-proton colliders with center-of-mass energies of 27 and 100 TeV, and future lepton colliders operating at various energy levels. (QPNet), a pitch-adaptive neural network designed to enhance the limited pitch-invariance of standard WaveNet (WN) through the integration of complex-valued, quasi-periodic complex neural networks (QPCNNs). While a basic QPNet architecture serves as a pitch-adaptive variant of WN, an extended version, the multi-rate QPNet (MQPNet), extends this capability by functioning as a multi-scale WN and offering greater flexibility via complex-valued convolutional layers (CLs) at various rates. Both QPNet and MQPNet maintain a non-autoregressive structure identical to WN, supporting mini-batch training and efficient implementation using cuDNN and GPU acceleration. Despite its architectural similarity to WN, QPNet demonstrates superior or equivalent performance across diverse pitch-adapted TTS tasks. Specifically, in the LibTTS benchmark, QPnet achieves a 0.6 CMOS improvement, and MQPnet yields a 0.4 CMOS improvement, surpassing WN. Similarly, in the TTS-Pitch Tuning (TTS-PT) benchmark, QPnet provides a 12.62 dB mean improvement, and MQPnet yields a 5.79 dB improvement over WN. All code, models, and data utilized in these evaluations are publicly released. Code: https://github.com/ognn/TTS-Pitch-PitchAdapt-WaveNet Star.

However, a significant limitation of the current QPNet is its increased computational cost compared to WN, resulting from the use of complex-valued CLs. To address this, we propose accelerating these complex-valued CLs by 2.2 times using 128-bit quantization, a method previously successful in periodic neural networks (PNNs). Furthermore, 128-bit quantization reduces memory usage by more than 50%. This optimization not only accelerates QPNet to match the speed of WN but also offers a more memory-efficient solution than WN, yielding the same or better results in both the LibTTS and TTS-PT benchmarks. The early M-dwarf b-K2V star system, identified around a decade ago, stood out because its second star is unusually rare among close binaries: it is an exact mirror image of its partner, possessing equal mass, radius, and radius ratio. The question arises whether the gravitational influence of such a symmetric configuration exerts extra stress on planet detection. Our analysis reveals that when activity signals are uncorrected and equal, this configuration does generate additional radial velocity noise. However, since activity signals are rarely consistent, such a geometry actually offers an advantage by allowing astronomers to more effectively isolate and remove the impact of accreting spots and faculae. We conclude that among all possible stellar activity scenarios, a binary system with two identical stars represents a favorable configuration for finding exoplanets. Approximately 5% of known exoplanet hosts around M-dwarfs exhibit a secondary component with a mass ratio close to unity. We estimate the average enhancement factor for radial velocity noise in these systems to be approximately 0.8. Our findings also extend to systems involving equal-mass giants or black holes, suggesting this geometry is universally beneficial for planet detection. This could help explain the higher frequency of planetary detections around close-double-star systems compared to single stars of equivalent spectral type. Furthermore, we anticipate that the continued discovery of systems featuring two equal stars will contribute to testing hypotheses in astrophysics, including those within the field of numerical relativity. Finally, we examine the statistical significance of a recently discovered super-Earth orbiting the system BPS J0853+3927, which serves as a new example of a host star with two equal stars. This discovery reinforces our conclusion, as the planet was detected using data from one of the most rigorous exoplanet surveys. The existence of Earth-mass bodies around stars with two equal stars now supports a model of planetary systems with increased structure and complexity. Such systems include the solar system, which contains eight planets, numerous minor planets, a dense cluster of satellite systems around the giant planets, and a halo of thousands of stellar-mass black holes. The emergence of planetary systems could therefore be characterized by an elevated degree of structure and complexity. This hypothesis offers a new perspective for explaining why so many exoplanets have been discovered thus far. Both the hypothesis and the alternative view, which attributes the exoplanetic puzzle to pure chance, are currently testable.

In this study, we experimentally confirm the robust generation of spin-orbit coupling in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ through nanofabrication. We demonstrate that simply depositing a thin film of CrO$_2$ or LaAlO$_3$ on the semiconductor's surface is sufficient to induce this effect. This engineered spin-orbit coupling is essential for supporting topological Andreev bound states at the interface of a spin-orbit coupled semiconductor and a superconductor. We characterize these states using a tunneling microscope by probing the local density of states at the bi-material boundary with a metallic tip. Under ideal conditions, we observe a significant zero bias peak signifying a bound state at the gap edge, which aligns well with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we illustrate that this specific setup provides a new platform for investigating topological Andreev bound states and for the potential manipulation of Majorana modes. This process involves generating a internal representation (state) of the external world and formulating actions to achieve a specific utility function. The inferences required for active inference encompass both the prediction of internal states given observations (perception) and the determination of actions to reach desired states (action). Similarly, the interaction with the environment is defined by the generation of observations in response to actions (perception) and the translation of internal state representations into external interactions (action). Traditionally, these interaction components have been recognized as part of the perception-action cycle, a core tenet of active perception. Despite its importance, an internal generative model that explicitly represents the dependence between state and action has not yet been developed. This paper addresses that gap by introducing a BERT-based active inference agent. This agent utilizes a neural network to jointly infer states and actions, which is then trained to develop an internal model of these interactions. The proposed approach is validated through a simulated robot task. Results demonstrate that the agent can effectively predict the effects of its actions on the environment and accurately interpret sensor data resulting from those actions. Furthermore, the agent achieves a level of task success comparable to a baseline approach that does not employ active inference. Currently, the method is restricted to deterministic environments and to situations where the probability of an observation remains constant regardless of the action taken. Future research will expand the approach's applicability to stochastic environments where observations may vary even when the state and action are known. To do this, the agent will be enhanced to predict observation variability and will be evaluated on a more complex robot manipulation benchmark. Furthermore, the method will be demonstrated on a real robotic arm. This will help illustrate the approach's potential to endow autonomous agents with more sophisticated active inference capabilities and better understand how the neural BERT model captures the internal relationships between states and actions. Ultimately, this formulation offers a unified perspective on active inference, bringing together previously separate strategies for action and perception into a single, coherent framework. During training, the agent is given a simple reward function to motivate the development of internal models of state-action interactions, a capability that goes beyond standard active inference and is difficult to acquire through supervision. Specifically, his decision to conduct a drop tower experiment—despite the existence of established mathematical methods for verifying the acceleration implied by the parabolic trajectory of projectiles—suggests an error in reasoning. By relying on an actual drop tower when a simpler, well-documented mathematical approach was available, Galileo may have inadvertently slowed the progression of mechanical science. More broadly, this paper examines the complex relationship between mathematics and experiment within physical research. It also contends that 19th- and 20th-century physicists, such as Newton, Einstein, and Eddington, were not necessarily superior in experimental design to their 17th-century counterparts like Galileo, Kepler, and Descartes. Ultimately, the true engine of scientific advancement is mathematics, but only as a precise and rigorous language; its practical application remains an imprecise and uncertain art.

This study employs the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code Open-XPSD and presents a kinetic scale model demonstrating the connection between island coalescence and the formation of Alfvénic solitons. The simulation utilizes a $64^3$ grid (previously insufficient for island coalescence studies) within a box $8D_{i,0}$ deep, where $D_{i,0}=2c_{A,0}/\Omega_{c,i}$, $c_{A,0}$ is the Alfvén speed, $\Omega_{c,i}$ is the ion gyrofrequency, and the field is $B_0\hat{z}$. Initially, two $D_{i,0}/4$ magnetic islands are positioned at $\pm D_{i,0}/4\hat{x}$, creating an antiparallel discontinuity across the Alfvén distance $2D_{i,0}$. The open boundaries allow plasma to escape, forming a cusp configuration that generates open X-point magnetic topologies in all eight octants. Our results show solutions approaching the kinetic scale $c_{A,0}\Omega_{c,i}$ and indicate the first time island coalescence in open magnetic topologies has been simulated. Initially, magnetic flux ropes rapidly form between the two islands, while plasma is funneled toward the magnetic axes, creating thin current sheets that trigger ion and electron pair instabilities (agile two-stream and two-dimensional modified two-temperature mirror instabilities). These instabilities rapidly deplete energy and particle acceleration. Consequently, magnetic islands break, fragment into smaller structures, and split into magnetic ropes. Currents pinch, causing the islands to fragment into island-ropes that oscillate stably. The front and back magnetic fields transition to cusp configurations, while new island-ropes between the initial islands form solenoidal magnetic field structures. Fast reconnection occurs rapidly, with the time scale matching the Agreed time scale. Fast reconnection and island fragmentation release free energy, exciting Agreed instabilities that generate Alfvénic structures. Fast island fragmentation produces Alfvénic structures (solitons) that oscillate stably for many ion periods. Fast reformation behind the initial magnetic islands creates island-ropes that evolve into Alfvénic structures. In this paper, we introduce a novel memory mechanism for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), termed the Gating Network for RNNs (GaNet). By utilizing additional layer-based gates, GaNet selectively retains and discards both short-term and long-term information within RNN hidden states. We extend this concept to transform a standard RNN into a compact, memory-efficient, and energy-efficient neural network known as the GnRNN. Beyond its application in memory management, the GnRNN demonstrates superior performance in speech recognition, image classification, and next character prediction compared to standard RNNs, particularly when trained with limited data. Our results indicate that the integration of gate layers enhances learning efficiency by regulating memory, reducing redundancy, and maintaining long-term information. We further show that the gate layers can be effectively pruned post-training to lower power consumption, resulting in a more streamlined network. We open-source our code at https://github.com/azadmoaven/GaNet-RNN and provide data for limited-data training scenarios at the same repository
